順天府鄉試錄序

惟我皇上御極十有三年秋七月壬申，渙頒大號，建閣開館，爰以光昭列聖寶訓實錄，乃特命臣道南爲管錄官，臣衮爲校錄官。越八月辛丑，順天府疏請賓興多士，如恒期。上申命臣道南、臣衮蹔輟史局，往司文柄，爲考試官。先是聘至同考
translation_en:
Preface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In autumn, on the renshen day of the seventh month of the thirteenth year of our Emperor’s reign, His Majesty solemnly issued a grand proclamation, establishing a pavilion and opening a compilation office to bring to light the Precious Instructions and Veritable Records of the successive sage emperors. He specially appointed your servant Daonan as Official in Charge of Transcription and your servant Gun as Collating Official. Subsequently, on the xinchou day of the eighth month, Shuntian Prefecture submitted a memorial requesting that the examination to select worthy scholars be held at the customary time. His Majesty then ordered your servants Daonan and Gun temporarily to suspend their work in the historiographical office and go to preside over the literary selection as Examiners. Before this, those who had been invited and had arrived to serve as Associate Examiners …

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
則臣塾臣汶臣勛臣廷吉臣正
臣應奎臣良臣錫臣琯監試則
臣學孔臣釋而提調茲試則臣
漢也是月也提學御史臣方一
桂所選畿甸士及黌宮省署雲
集而試者凡三千人三試之拔
其雋者凡百三十有五人遵
===
成憲也臣伏惟我
朝養士之厚教士之豫選士之備
蓋監諸成周臣請以周爲監可
乎昔者后稷公劉以稼穡起家
太王王季以忠厚立國越若文
武則又以道德植綱紀以綱紀
培教化以教化淑人才以人才

則臣塾、臣汶、臣勛、臣廷吉、臣正、臣應奎、臣良、臣錫、臣琯；監試則臣學孔、臣釋，而提調茲試則臣漢也。是月也，提學御史臣方一桂所選畿甸士及黌宮省署雲集，而試者凡三千人。三試之，拔其雋者凡百三十有五人，遵成憲也。
臣伏惟我朝養士之厚、教士之豫、選士之備，蓋監諸成周。臣請以周爲監，可乎？昔者后稷、公劉以稼穡起家，太王、王季以忠厚立國。越若文、武，則又以道德植綱紀，以綱紀培教化，以教化淑人才，以人才
translation_en:
…were your servants Shu, Wen, Xun, Tingji, Zheng, Yingkui, Liang, Xi, and Guan. Supervising the examination were your servants Xuekong and Shi, while your servant Han served as Proctor for this examination. That month, scholars of the capital region selected by your servant Fang Yigui, Education Inspector, together with those from the schools and government offices [?], gathered like clouds. In all, three thousand men sat the examination. They were examined in three sessions, and the outstanding among them, numbering one hundred and thirty-five, were selected in accordance with established regulations.
Your servant humbly considers that our dynasty’s generous nurture of scholars, their education well in advance, and the thoroughness of their selection take the accomplished Zhou as their model. May your servant therefore ask to take Zhou as a mirror? In ancient times, Hou Ji and Gong Liu established their house through agriculture; King Tai and King Ji founded their state upon loyalty and generosity. Coming to Kings Wen and Wu, they further used the Way and virtue to establish the governing framework, that framework to foster moral instruction, moral instruction to improve men of talent, and men of talent to…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
贊治理是故自黨庠術序瞽宗
米廩以達于辟雝養之不可謂
不厚矣自辨志樂群博習論學
以底于大成教之不可謂不豫
矣自敬敏任恤孝弟睦婣以稽
于德藝選之不可謂不備矣是
故論定後官任官後爵位定後
===
祿宅俊兼收浚亮克乂茂績淵
猷穆哉休矣詩曰濟濟多士文
王以寧又曰桓桓武王保有厥
士可不謂得士之盛爾矣乎恭
惟我
玄皇
恒皇懋昭明德

===
祿宅俊乂收浚亮克乂茂績淵
猷穆哉休矣詩曰濟濟多士文
王以寧又曰桓桓武王保有厥
士可不謂得士之盛爾矣乎恭
惟我
玄皇
恒皇懋昭明德
punctuated:
贊治理。是故自黨庠、術序、瞽宗、米廩，以達于辟雝，養之不可謂不厚矣；自辨志樂群、博習論學，以底于大成，教之不可謂不豫矣；自敬敏任恤、孝弟睦婣，以稽于德藝，選之不可謂不備矣。是故論定後官，任官後爵，位定後祿。宅俊兼收，浚亮克乂，茂績淵猷，穆哉休矣！詩曰：「濟濟多士，文王以寧。」又曰：「桓桓武王，保有厥士。」可不謂得士之盛爾矣乎？
恭惟我玄皇、恒皇，懋昭明德，
translation_en:
…to assist in governing. Thus, from the local xiang and xu schools, through the Guzong and Milin schools, up to the royal Biyong academy, their nurturing of scholars could hardly be called ungenerous. From discerning their aspirations and learning to associate harmoniously with others, through extensive study and discussion of learning, to full accomplishment, their instruction could hardly be called lacking in advance preparation. By examining reverence, diligence, trustworthiness, compassion, filial devotion, respect for elder brothers, harmony among kin, and amity among relatives by marriage, and assessing virtue and cultivated skills, their selection could hardly be called incomplete. Thus, only after assessments were settled were men appointed to office; only after appointment were they granted rank; and only after their positions were determined were they granted emoluments. Worthy men were placed in office and broadly admitted; profound and discerning, they were capable of governing. Their achievements were splendid and their plans far-reaching. How august and glorious! The Book of Odes says: “Numerous were the worthy men; through them King Wen enjoyed peace.” It also says: “Valiant King Wu retained his worthy men.” Could this not be called a flourishing age for obtaining worthy men?
We reverently reflect that our Emperor Xuan and Emperor Heng assiduously made manifest their luminous virtue…

淳皇肇啟峻業視周后稷公劉太王
王季其揆一也我
太祖高皇帝統天馭宇惇隆六籍罷
黜百家
太宗文皇帝纂曆遷鼎勵精幾務銳

===

京師赫聲濯靈爲四方極山祇毓

裕皇、淳皇肇啟峻業，視周后稷、公劉、太王、王季，其揆一也。我太祖高皇帝統天馭宇，惇隆六籍，罷黜百家；太宗文皇帝纂曆遷鼎，勵精幾務，銳情經典，視周文武，又有若合符節焉者。
我皇上祇承列聖，覲光揚烈，化軌覃宣，士習嚮正。日際月域，罔弗丕冒。矧京師赫聲濯靈，爲四方極！山祇毓祉，川若効禎，物采既章，人文載賁，彬彬然甲于成周之盛矣。臣
translation_en:
…Emperor Yu and Emperor Chun inaugurated the great enterprise; measured against Hou Ji, Gong Liu, King Tai, and King Ji of Zhou, they followed the same principles. Our Emperor Taizu Gao ruled all beneath Heaven and governed the realm, greatly honoring the Six Classics and rejecting the Hundred Schools. Emperor Taizong Wen succeeded to the imperial mandate and transferred the capital, devoting his energies to the critical affairs of government and setting his heart firmly upon the classics. Compared with Kings Wen and Wu of Zhou, he likewise matched them as closely as the two halves of a tally.
Our reigning emperor reverently carries on the legacy of the sage emperors, beholding their radiance and spreading the glory of their achievements. The patterns of his transforming influence extend far and wide, and the habits of scholars turn toward rectitude. To the limits reached by sun and moon, none fail to receive his abundant protection. How much more so in the capital, whose resounding renown and brilliant spiritual power make it the guiding standard for the four quarters! Mountain spirits nurture blessings, and river spirits present auspicious signs. The splendor of the material world is manifest, and human culture adds its ornament. Such cultivated flourishing surpasses even the heyday of Chengzhou. Your servant…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
又聞之召公告成王曰藹藹王
多吉士維君子使媚于天子蓋
言爲上爲德也藹藹王多吉人
維君子命媚于庶人蓋言爲下
爲民也爾多士沐兹
純化觀光利賓荷兹
豐寵拔茅連彙嗣是而自靖自獻
===

重教之者豫則其自修也必力
選之者備則其自靖自獻于
廷者必將爲馮爲翼爲孝爲德以
樹迺則爲藩爲垣爲屏爲翰以

translation_en: …have also heard that the Duke of Shao admonished King Cheng, saying: “In abundance, the king has many worthy officers; they are gentlemen whom he employs, who win the affection of the Son of Heaven.” This speaks of serving those above and advancing virtue. “In abundance, the king has many worthy men; they are gentlemen whom he commissions, who win the affection of the common people.” This speaks of serving those below and working for the people. You assembled scholars have been steeped in this pure moral transformation, have beheld the glory of the realm and enjoyed the privilege of appearing as guests at court, and have received this abundant favor. Like clumps of thatch pulled up together by their intertwined roots, you have advanced in company. title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹塲
四書
寬則得衆信則民任焉敏則有功公則說
夫孝者善繼人之志善述人之事者也春
秋修其祖廟陳其宗器設其裳衣薦其
時食宗廟之禮所以序昭穆也序爵所
以辨貴賤也序事所以辨賢也旅酬下
爲上所以逮賤也燕毛所以序齒也踐

Four Books

If you are generous, you will win the multitude; if trustworthy, the people will entrust you with responsibility; if diligent, you will achieve results; if impartial, you will bring satisfaction.

Filial devotion consists in skillfully carrying on the intentions of one’s forebears and skillfully continuing their undertakings. In spring and autumn, descendants put their ancestral temples in order, display their ancestral vessels, lay out their ancestors’ ceremonial robes, and offer seasonal foods. The rites of the ancestral temple establish the order of the zhao and mu generations. Ordering participants by noble rank distinguishes the exalted from the lowly; assigning ritual duties distinguishes the worthy. In the general exchange of toasts, those below offer to those above, so that even the lowly are included. At the banquet, arranging places by the color of the participants’ hair establishes precedence by age. They occupy their forebears’ places, perform their rites, play their music, revere those whom they honored, and love those whom they held dear.

High though Heaven is, and distant though the stars are, if one seeks the principles underlying their movements, one can calculate the solstices a thousand years hence without leaving one’s seat.

The sun and moon adhere to Heaven; the grains, grasses, and trees adhere to the earth. Repeated brightness adhering to what is correct thus transforms and brings order to all under Heaven.

Six in the fourth place: Dispersing one’s group brings supreme good fortune. Through dispersal there is a mound—something beyond ordinary thought.

When the sages of antiquity made the Changes, they gave hidden assistance to the spiritual powers and brought forth the use of yarrow stalks. They assigned three to Heaven and two to Earth and based the numbers upon these. Observing changes in yin and yang, they established the trigrams…

…men of renown and treat the worthy with ritual respect.
Thus, human feelings are the field cultivated by the sage king.
When a king’s achievements are accomplished, he creates music; when his governance is settled, he establishes rites. The greater his achievements, the more fully developed his music; the more orderly his governance, the more complete his rites.
When the ancients established rites, they took Heaven and Earth as their guiding framework, the sun and moon as their ordering pattern, and the three luminaries as their further reference: these are the foundations of government and instruction.

These records bear the weighty responsibility of transmitting counsels and instructions to their contemporaries and bequeathing guides and examples to later generations. As for the Han dynasty’s Huguan and Shiqu, the Tang dynasty’s Jixian and Lizheng, and the Song dynasty’s Chongzheng and Erying, discussions of the classics and histories held there frequently touched on affairs of government. Might the words and actions on those occasions also merit recording?

Our Emperor Taizu Gao’s words, recorded in the Precious Instructions, serve as models for all under Heaven through successive generations; his deeds, recorded in the Precious Record, likewise serve as standards for all under Heaven through successive generations. 祀者有謂祫爲祖孫尊屈又有以爲服
畢之祭者其於春秋所特書者果同乎
punctuated:
《聖政日曆》及《皇明政要》，此則諸生所誦習焉者。如御華蓋殿論易，武英殿論書，及論大學、論孟，是皆論經而有及於傳者也。如御白虎殿論漢史，左閤論宋史，及論唐史、元史，是皆論史而有及於政者也。聖謨洋洋，嘉言孔彰，諸生其對揚之，以光昭我皇上法祖之休烈。
問：禮莫嚴於祭祀，義莫深於禘祫。古今之論二禮者多矣。有謂禘兼郊廟，又有以為追遠者；有謂禘審昭穆，又有以為特祭者。其於孔子所不知者，果知之否歟？有謂祫為骨肉合食，又有以為列尸之祀者；有謂祫為祖孫尊屈，又有以為服畢之祭者。其於春秋所特書者，果同乎
translation_en:
…the Daily Record of Sagely Governance (Shengzheng rili) and the Essentials of Government of the August Ming (Huang Ming zhengyao): these are works that you candidates recite and study. Examples include discussions of the Changes while holding court in Huagai Hall, of the Documents in Wuying Hall, and of the Great Learning, the Analects, and the Mencius. All these were discussions of the classics that also touched upon their commentaries. Examples also include discussions of Han history while holding court in Baihu Hall, of Song history in the Left Pavilion, and of Tang and Yuan history. All these were discussions of history that also touched upon government. The sage sovereign’s counsels are abundant, and his excellent sayings are conspicuously manifest. You candidates should expound and extol them in your answers, thereby illuminating the splendid achievements of our Emperor in following his ancestors.
Question: Among rites, none is more solemn than sacrifice; in significance, none is more profound than the di and xia ancestral sacrifices. Many, past and present, have discussed these two rites. Some say that di encompasses both suburban and ancestral-temple sacrifices; others take it to mean tracing back to distant ancestors. Some say that di distinguishes the zhao and mu ancestral ranks; others regard it as a special sacrifice. Do they truly understand what Confucius professed not to know? Some say that xia is a shared meal among blood relatives; others regard it as a sacrifice with an array of ancestral impersonators. Some say that xia involves the yielding of precedence between ancestors and descendants [?]; others regard it as a sacrifice upon completion of mourning. Does what they describe truly accord with what the Spring and Autumn Annals specifically recorded …

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
否歟至於宋儒折衷固有定論其詳亦
可得聞歟恭惟
皇上肇舉
大禘之祭重定
大袷之圖真建諸天地而不悖質諸鬼神而無
疑焉者諸生稽古待問久矣其敬陳之
問堯命羲和授時舜命后夔典樂曆律之
關於治道大矣三代而下論曆律者無
慮數十百家乃若唐之一行論氣朔推
===
步者凡七議曆數者十有二其術可得
聞歟至元郭守敬獨取而廣演之亦有
得於一行之術乎否歟宋之沅定述律
呂證辨者凡十論本原者十有三其學
固有所自歟至朱氏門人又從而考訂
之亦有取於元定之學乎否歟方
今
聖人在上治曆以明時制樂以崇古諸生必有
究心於是者願詳言之毋泛毋畧

punctuated:
否歟？至於宋儒折衷，固有定論，其詳亦可得聞歟？恭惟皇上肇舉大禘之祭，重定大袷之圖，真建諸天地而不悖，質諸鬼神而無疑焉者。諸生稽古待問久矣，其敬陳之。

問：堯命羲和授時，舜命后夔典樂，曆律之關於治道大矣。三代而下，論曆律者無慮數十百家。乃若唐之一行，論氣朔推步者凡七，議曆數者十有二，其術可得聞歟？至元郭守敬獨取而廣演之，亦有得於一行之術乎否歟？宋之沅定，述律呂證辨者凡十，論本原者十有三，其學固有所自歟？至朱氏門人又從而考訂之，亦有取於元定之學乎否歟？方今聖人在上，治曆以明時，制樂以崇古。諸生必有究心於是者，願詳言之，毋泛毋畧。
translation_en:
…or not? As for the balanced judgments of the Song Confucian scholars, there are certainly settled conclusions. May we also hear their details? We reverently reflect that His Majesty has inaugurated the great di sacrifice and revised the diagram of the great collective ancestral sacrifice (qia; transcribed as 袷). These are truly measures that may be established before Heaven and Earth without contradiction and tested before the spirits without doubt. You candidates have long studied antiquity in readiness for questioning; respectfully present your accounts.

Question: Yao commanded Xi and He to determine and announce the seasons; Shun commanded Hou Kui to direct music. Calendrical astronomy and musical pitch standards thus bear greatly upon the art of government. Since the Three Dynasties, those who have discussed these subjects number in the scores or hundreds. As for Yixing of the Tang, his discussions of calculating solar terms and new moons comprised seven sections, and his deliberations on calendrical numbers comprised twelve. May we hear about his methods? Later, in the Yuan dynasty, Guo Shoujing singled these out and developed them extensively. Did he also gain insights from Yixing’s methods, or not? Yuanding of the Song (here transcribed as 沅定 [?]) wrote ten sections demonstrating and distinguishing musical pitch standards and thirteen discussing their fundamental origins. Surely his learning had a source? Subsequently, disciples of Master Zhu further examined and revised this work. Did they also draw upon Yuanding’s learning, or not? Now that a sage occupies the throne, he regulates the calendar to clarify the seasons and establishes music to honor antiquity. Among you candidates there must be those who have studied these matters attentively. Please discuss them in detail, without vagueness or omissions.

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
問宋儒真德秀讀書記為集有四其乙集之
所載專叙歷代名臣事業而以四事考
其是非優劣上下數千載間治亂興衰
之跡炳然見矣姑以漢唐言之史稱蕭
曹丙魏房杜姚宋其名最著自是而下
或以經術文學或以勲德才猷亦各表
盛一時有裨國政而史氏不取之以並
賛何歟他如王佐之才經濟之學先儒
皆極稱許而事功成就顧若後焉其故
===
何也真氏兼採而並錄之間以已意而
加斷焉數公之中質之四事無歉者果
何人為稱首歟孟子曰誦其詩讀其書
不知其人可乎是以論其世也諸士抱
負墳策尚友古人其於漢唐諸臣之得
失必有槩於中久矣願具言之以觀經
世之志
問天下一體也內而邦畿外而郡縣厥重
均矣古今言治者自郡縣始漢唐中世

世之志

均矣古今言治者自郡縣始漢唐中世
punctuated:
問：宋儒真德秀《讀書記》為集有四，其乙集之所載，專叙歷代名臣事業，而以四事考其是非優劣。上下數千載間治亂興衰之跡，炳然見矣。姑以漢唐言之，史稱蕭、曹、丙、魏、房、杜、姚、宋，其名最著。自是而下，或以經術文學，或以勲德才猷，亦各表盛一時，有裨國政，而史氏不取之以並賛，何歟？他如王佐之才、經濟之學，先儒皆極稱許，而事功成就顧若後焉，其故何也？真氏兼採而並錄之，間以已意而加斷焉。數公之中，質之四事，無歉者果何人為稱首歟？孟子曰：「誦其詩，讀其書，不知其人，可乎？是以論其世也。」諸士抱負墳策，尚友古人，其於漢唐諸臣之得失，必有槩於中久矣。願具言之，以觀經世之志。

問：天下一體也，內而邦畿，外而郡縣，厥重均矣。古今言治者，自郡縣始。漢唐中世
translation_en:
Question: The Song Confucian scholar Zhen Dexiu’s Reading Notes (Dushu ji) comprises four collections. The second collection records exclusively the deeds and achievements of eminent ministers through successive dynasties, assessing their right and wrong, strengths and weaknesses, by four criteria. Thus the traces of order and disorder, rise and decline, over several thousand years stand clearly revealed. Taking just the Han and Tang as examples, the histories speak of Xiao He, Cao Shen, Bing Ji, Wei Xiang, Fang Xuanling, Du Ruhui, Yao Chong, and Song Jing, whose names are the most celebrated. Below these men, others distinguished themselves in their own times through classical learning and literary scholarship, or through meritorious service, virtue, ability, and counsel, and contributed to the government of the state. Why, then, did the historians not select them for praise alongside these men? Others possessed the ability to assist a true king and the learning needed to order the realm—qualities that earlier Confucian scholars praised most highly—yet their practical accomplishments seem to have fallen behind. Why was this?

Zhen included and recorded them all, occasionally adding judgments based on his own views. Among these gentlemen, who, when measured against the four criteria and found wanting in none, truly deserves to rank first? Mencius said: “Can one recite their poems and read their writings without knowing what sort of people they were? Hence one examines the age in which they lived.” You scholars cherish the ancient writings and seek friendship with the ancients. Surely you have long formed judgments in your minds concerning the successes and failures of these ministers of the Han and Tang. Set these out fully, so that we may see your aspirations for ordering the world.

Question: All under Heaven forms a single body. The capital region within and the commanderies and counties beyond are equally important. Those who have discussed governance, ancient and modern, have begun with the commanderies and counties. During the middle periods of the Han and Tang dynasties…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其間願治之君往往皆重刺史之選思
與共理或形之歎息欲考其人與政至
錄姓名于屏風卧興對之甚者治郡不
進詰責加焉才否狀白即擬廢置若此
可謂深識治體矣神爵五鳳之間貞觀
之際果各有所稱述否乎當時公卿之
徵拜才否之廢置赫然以循良見稱者
可數而評之歟唐臣有取於漢事也以
之進諫其君宋臣復有取於唐事也以
===
之進讀邇英其說可得聞歟或又謂令
兼五善之難或又慮非皆賢也議立八
條以察吏治不知其所論議亦有可采
者乎執事者願有聞也

punctuated: 其間願治之君，往往皆重刺史之選，思與共理，或形之歎息。欲考其人與政，至錄姓名于屏風，卧興對之。甚者治郡不進，詰責加焉；才否狀白，即擬廢置。若此，可謂深識治體矣。神爵、五鳳之間，貞觀之際，果各有所稱述否乎？當時公卿之徵拜、才否之廢置，赫然以循良見稱者，可數而評之歟？唐臣有取於漢事也，以之進諫其君；宋臣復有取於唐事也，以之進讀邇英，其說可得聞歟？或又謂令兼五善之難，或又慮非皆賢也，議立八條以察吏治，不知其所論議亦有可采者乎？執事者願有聞也。
translation_en:
…Among them, rulers who aspired to good government often attached great importance to selecting regional inspectors, hoping to share the work of governing with them; some expressed this longing in sighs. Wishing to examine these men and their administration, they went so far as to record their names on a screen, facing it upon retiring and rising. Some went further: when a commandery’s administration failed to improve, they subjected its administrator to questioning and reprimand; once the facts concerning his competence or incompetence became clear, they promptly considered dismissal or appointment. Such conduct may be said to show a profound understanding of the essentials of government.

During the Shenjue and Wufeng reign periods, and during the Zhenguan reign period, were there indeed achievements worthy of praise in each? Among the high ministers summoned and appointed at those times, and the officials dismissed or appointed according to their competence, can those conspicuously praised for conscientious and benevolent administration be enumerated and assessed?

A Tang minister drew upon precedents from the Han to remonstrate with his ruler; a Song minister in turn drew upon precedents from the Tang to present a reading before the emperor in the Yingying Hall. May we hear their arguments? Some also spoke of the difficulty of a county magistrate possessing all five good qualities; others, concerned that not all officials were worthy, proposed establishing eight articles for scrutinizing their administration. Might there be something worth adopting in these discussions and proposals? Those conducting this examination would welcome your views.

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
第壹場
四書
寬則得衆信則民任焉敏則有功公則說
楊周
同考試官教諭陳批是篇說出帝王傳心
之學尤為親切可以為文矣
同考試官教授唐批以寬信敏公本諸聖學
而達於政事卓有所見宜錄之
考試官侍讀張批典雅
===
考試官侍講學士廖批簡明
記者統言帝王致治之道以明聖學之傳也蓋
道之所貴者中觀帝王致治以中聖學傳心之
要見矣夫堯舜禹大聖人也湯武亦大聖人也
其道豈有二哉一中而已以言乎居上也含弘
而不迫從容而有制其道寬矣夫惟寬也而後
衆歸之四方丕應合其散而萃其離戴之惟恐
後也衆其有不得乎以言乎臨下也真實而無
妄終始而有恒其道信矣夫惟信也而後民任

punctuated:
第壹場
四書
「寬則得衆，信則民任焉，敏則有功，公則說。」
楊周
同考試官教諭陳批：「是篇說出帝王傳心之學，尤為親切，可以為文矣。」
同考試官教授唐批：「以寬信敏公本諸聖學，而達於政事，卓有所見，宜錄之。」
考試官侍讀張批：「典雅。」
考試官侍講學士廖批：「簡明。」
記者統言帝王致治之道，以明聖學之傳也。蓋道之所貴者中，觀帝王致治以中，聖學傳心之要見矣。夫堯舜禹，大聖人也；湯武，亦大聖人也。其道豈有二哉？一中而已。以言乎居上也，含弘而不迫，從容而有制，其道寬矣。夫惟寬也，而後衆歸之，四方丕應，合其散而萃其離，戴之惟恐後也，衆其有不得乎？以言乎臨下也，真實而無妄，終始而有恒，其道信矣。夫惟信也，而後民任
translation_en:
First Session
Four Books
“When generous, one wins the multitude; when trustworthy, one is relied upon by the people; when diligent, one achieves results; when impartial, one brings contentment.”
Yang Zhou
Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor, comments: “This essay articulates the learning transmitted from mind to mind among the sage emperors and kings. Its treatment is particularly apt and direct: this may indeed be called a worthy composition.”
Associate Examiner Tang, Professor, comments: “It roots generosity, trustworthiness, diligence, and impartiality in the learning of the sages and extends them to governmental affairs. It displays outstanding insight and merits inclusion.”
Examiner Zhang, Reader-in-Waiting, comments: “Classical and elegant.”
Examiner Liao, Academician Expositor-in-Waiting, comments: “Concise and clear.”
The recorder speaks comprehensively of the way by which the sage emperors and kings brought about good government, thereby illuminating the transmission of the learning of the sages. What is prized in the Way is the Mean. When we observe how the sage emperors and kings brought about good government through the Mean, the essential principle of the transmission of the sages’ learning from mind to mind becomes apparent. Yao, Shun, and Yu were great sages; Tang and Wu were also great sages. Could their ways have differed? There was only the one Mean.
Speaking of occupying the position above others: embracing all with magnanimity, without pressing them; acting with composure, yet maintaining due regulation—such a way is generous. Only through generosity does the multitude turn to the ruler. The four quarters respond in full; the scattered are brought together and the separated gathered in. They uphold him, fearing only that they might lag behind. How could he fail to win the multitude?
Speaking of presiding over those below: being genuine and free from falsehood, constant from beginning to end—such a way is trustworthy. Only through trustworthiness do the people rely …

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之萬邦惟懷遠有望而近不厭倚之有所恃也
民其有不任乎乃若明作以成天下之務道存
乎敏也敏則果斷而罔艱易從而可久於是乎
庶事康焉庶績凝焉其功也大矣順應以通天
下之志道存乎公也公則大同而無我顯比而
忘私於是乎百官和焉百姓親焉其悅也至矣
是則中也者本諸心者也寬也信也敏也公也
達諸治者也帝王相授守一道蓋如此抑於是
而知孔子之集大成矣觀其贊堯曰大哉舜曰
===
君哉禹曰無間然矣湯武則曰順天應人矣蓋
遠宗近法實繼群聖之傳而心學於是乎在矣
事功固不待論也故曰先聖後聖其揆一也
夫孝者善繼人之志善述人之事者也春
秋修其祖廟陳其宗器設其裳衣薦其
時食宗廟之禮所以序昭穆也序爵所
以辨貴賤也序事所以辨賢也旅酬下
為上所以逮賤也燕毛所以序齒也踐
其位行其禮奏其樂敬其所尊愛其所

Diligence brings decisiveness without difficulty; such conduct is easy to follow and can endure. Thus the many affairs are well ordered and the many achievements firmly established. In tracing why the sages’ filial piety was consummate, the Doctrine of the Mean necessarily sets forth fully the rites of ancestral sacrifice and elaborates their meaning. Nothing in filial piety is greater than sacrificing to one’s ancestors. The sages instituted rites and provided for every particular: is this not what made their filial piety consummate? Why, then, were King Wu and the Duke of Zhou said to possess consummate filial piety? Where the former kings had intentions they wished to carry out but had not fulfilled, these successors skillfully continued their intentions, adapting their measures to suit the times. Where the former kings had accomplished deeds worthy of emulation, these successors skillfully carried those deeds forward, maintaining constant norms to preserve what was right.

How can this be seen? In the seasons of spring and autumn, they commenced pure sacrifices in the ancestral temples. Once rain and dew had moistened the earth, they put the timbers in order; once frost and dew had descended, they attended reverently to the temple structures. They also displayed the ancestral vessels to show their preservation of the inheritance, and laid out the robes to clothe the personator of the dead. translation_en:
…such was their expression of reverence toward their ancestors. Once the ancestral temple was established, the zhao and mu generations were arranged in proper order: reverently attending on the left, they ordered the zhao group; hastening to serve on the right, they ordered the mu group. They further arranged participants by rank to distinguish the noble from the lowly, and assigned ritual duties to distinguish the worthy. In the general exchange of toasts, those below offered to those above, fully expressing the concern that extended even to the lowly. At the banquet, seating followed the seniority indicated by hair color, with the young placed after their elders, strengthening respect for age. Such was their expression of love toward descendants, ministers, and common people. Thus the positions they occupied were those of the former kings, and the rites they performed and music they played were those of the former kings. Reverence extended to their ancestors: honoring the honored, it reached the spirits in the unseen realm. Love extended to descendants, ministers, and common people: cherishing their kin, it reached human beings in the visible realm. All these were excellent ways of carrying on their predecessors’ intentions and perpetuating their undertakings. Could they have achieved this without consummate filial piety? The Record of Rites says: “Only a sage can offer sacrifice to the Lord on High; only a filial son can offer sacrifice to his parents.” King Wu and the Duke of Zhou not only established ancestral temples to offer sacrifice to their ancestors, but also instituted the suburban and soil-altar sacrifices to worship Heaven and Earth. Ah! This was how the sages comprehended the foundations of ritual and music. Hence it is said: “When the great man puts ritual and music into practice, Heaven and Earth will thereby be made manifest.”
“High though Heaven is, distant though the stars are, if one seeks the principles underlying them, one can determine the solstices a thousand years hence without leaving one’s seat.”
Ouyang Die 歐陽昳

Associate Examiner Jiang, School Professor, comments: “His understanding of principle is clear and incisive, and his phrasing precise and apt. This is included to admonish those who engage in forced interpretations.”

The great worthy takes the Way of Heaven as his subject: by extrapolating from the past, one can know the future. Thus he shows people how to use their intelligence. The Way of Heaven is simply spontaneous. If one investigates what has already occurred, its principle will become apparent of itself. What need, then, is there for forced interpretation? Mencius feared that people discussing human nature would err through forced interpretation, and therefore offered this illustration. His meaning was roughly this: “I know why the study of human nature remains unclear: it is the fault of those who are clever. Why not investigate its established patterns?”

Heaven spreads its canopy above; nothing is higher. The stars display their forms suspended in heaven; nothing is more distant. Yet heaven has no bodily form of its own: it takes the celestial configurations as its form. Heaven has no measure of its own: it takes the celestial stations and lodges as its measure. Its established patterns can therefore be investigated. Why is this? Heaven is coordinated by reference to the sun, and the sun by reference to the stars. Heaven’s movement has a constant circuit, and the sun’s arrival at the solstice has a constant measure. Although the solar year has a surplus and the lunar months a shortfall, so that discrepancies sometimes arise, when the single yang returns, the Seven Regulators—the sun, moon, and five planets—follow it. The sun’s conjunction with the stellar station Xingji along its course will occur in the future just as it has in the past. Thus, even a thousand years hence may be calculated without rising from one’s seat. What difficulty, then, is there in investigating what is high and distant? 以成天下之化者有自矣且離之爲卦四陽二

天者天運神道以氣麗氣而貞明之體生焉蓋

translation_en:
…the meaning of its name. That celestial images and earthly forms depend upon the processes of creation and transformation is certainly so; yet human beings also participate in them. Thus there is a source from which their capacity to complete the transformation of all under Heaven derives. Now the hexagram Li (Clinging) has four yang lines and two yin lines: the yin cling to the yang. How may this be explained? The sun and moon form images in Heaven: Heaven sets its numinous Way in motion, vital energy clings to vital energy, and their enduringly luminous substance comes into being. The alternating courses of these two luminaries are the flowing activity of the Supreme Ultimate. The grains, grasses, and trees take form on Earth: Earth bears numinous vital energy, form clings to form, and the substance that sustains life takes shape. The full manifestation of the myriad things is the nurturing activity of Earth, represented by Kun. Such is certainly the case with creation and transformation; could human beings alone have nothing to which they cling?

Moreover, the meaning of Li is that both its upper and lower trigrams are Li, and its virtue is doubled illumination. Human beings truly possess this virtue. Thus there is the ruler, who presides over the transformation of all under Heaven. Able to illuminate his exalted virtue, he clings to the position in which he occupies the seat of rectitude: this corresponds to the way clinging operates in Heaven. There are ministers, who assist in the transformation of all under Heaven. They themselves make bright their luminous virtue and cling to offices that uphold rectitude: this corresponds to the way clinging operates on Earth. Hence ruler and ministers aid one another, and those above and below cultivate themselves in concert. They rectify the court in order to rectify the hundred officials, and fundamental transformation proceeds from this. Without favoritism or aversion, the myriad states will be brought into harmony. They rectify the hundred officials in order to rectify the myriad people, and great transformation flourishes. Without partiality or faction, all within the Four Seas will enjoy lasting peace. Is the means by which they transform and perfect all under Heaven not like the means by which Heaven and Earth accomplish their work of transformation?

Thus the Way of Heaven, the Way of Earth, and the Way of humanity share a single principle. Since human beings participate alongside Heaven and Earth, can they fail, each, to fulfill their proper Way? Furthermore, in this hexagram, the six in the fifth place is central and compliant…

天下之重任以其位則儲副也祗凝休命而群
子莫與齒焉以其分則世嫡也靈承純祐而族
人不敢戚焉是故震之為卦長子之象也震之
次鼎相承之序也陰陽始交而一陽交於二陰
之下六子之變化震其肇端矣乾坤相索而一
索居于二索之首兩儀之絪縕震其托始矣故
曰主器者莫若長子此震之所以次鼎也得無
意乎抑禮尊世子書重元子春秋之義立嫡以
長蓋天下之本在儲貳也古之聖王建為保傅

定鼎郟鄏矣胡為乎猶有問鼎如楚子者噫震
而已矣吾於鼎也何尤

…the weighty responsibility of All-under-Heaven. In rank, he is the heir apparent: he reverently upholds the glorious mandate, and none of the other sons can stand alongside him. In his allotted station, he is the principal heir: he auspiciously receives Heaven’s abundant blessings, and members of the lineage dare not presume upon their kinship. Thus, the hexagram Zhen (Thunder) represents the eldest son; its following Ding (the Cauldron) expresses the order of succession. When yin and yang first unite, one yang line joins beneath two yin lines: the transformations of the six children begin with Zhen. When Qian and Kun seek one another, the first seeking precedes the second: the generative intermingling of the two primal powers takes its beginning in Zhen. Hence it is said, “None is better suited to preside over the sacred vessels than the eldest son.” This is why Zhen follows Ding. Could this be without significance?

Moreover, the Rites honors the hereditary heir, the Documents accords weight to the eldest son, and the principle of the Spring and Autumn Annals is to establish the eldest among the sons of the principal wife as heir. For the foundation of All-under-Heaven lies in the heir apparent. The sage kings of antiquity established guardians, preceptors, advisers, and assistants to support him; thus the one who would preside over the vessels, as represented by Zhen, was securely established. Otherwise, although the house of Zhou had installed its cauldrons at Jiaru, why were there still men like the ruler of Chu who inquired about them? Alas! It is simply a matter of Zhen. What fault could I find with Ding?

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
之興也孰知文王爲之造乎是故成象於天莫
大乎日月光被下土莫大乎照臨我穆考文王
也以緝熈不已之誠致旁燭無疆之盛豈不與
日月同其照臨乎彼疆里之所區畫莫遠於四
方也但見文明之廣運萬物同仰其光輝宣哲
之流通百嘉咸遂乎鬯達無幽不格也無遠不
届也其光於四方有如此王迹之所肇造莫近
於西土也但見修和之化誕昭丕冒之恩奠麗
之澤聿興孔邇之頌令聞是孚也耿光是覲也
===
其顯於西土又如此是則西土曰顯四方曰光
非光不足於顯也特自其遠近者言之耳文王
之德天命人心所歸有以哉抑考周有天下后
稷啓之公劉太王王季繼之其積累締造非一
朝夕之故矣其受天命以有天下則自文王始
故泰誓三篇其命后誓眾之辭反覆乎文王之
德以見天佑人歸之本祖宗德澤可想見也周
家兆祚八百爲三代有道之長信夫

詩
punctuated:
之興也，孰知文王爲之造乎？是故成象於天，莫大乎日月；光被下土，莫大乎照臨。我穆考文王也，以緝熈不已之誠，致旁燭無疆之盛，豈不與日月同其照臨乎？彼疆里之所區畫，莫遠於四方也。但見文明之廣運，萬物同仰其光輝；宣哲之流通，百嘉咸遂乎鬯達。無幽不格也，無遠不届也，其光於四方有如此。王迹之所肇造，莫近於西土也。但見修和之化，誕昭丕冒之恩；奠麗之澤，聿興孔邇之頌。令聞是孚也，耿光是覲也，其顯於西土又如此。是則西土曰顯，四方曰光，非光不足於顯也，特自其遠近者言之耳。文王之德，天命人心所歸，有以哉！抑考周有天下，后稷啓之，公劉、太王、王季繼之，其積累締造，非一朝夕之故矣。其受天命以有天下，則自文王始。故《泰誓》三篇，其命后誓眾之辭，反覆乎文王之德，以見天佑人歸之本。祖宗德澤，可想見也。周家兆祚八百，爲三代有道之長，信夫！

詩
translation_en:
…in its rise, who understands that King Wen laid its foundations? Thus, among the forms manifested in Heaven, none are greater than the sun and moon; in spreading radiance over the earth below, nothing is greater than their illumination. My august deceased father, King Wen, through his sincerity in ceaselessly cultivating luminous virtue, achieved the splendor of illumination extending everywhere without limit. Did he not share the illuminating power of the sun and moon? Among the lands marked out by boundaries, none are more distant than the four quarters. Yet we see his cultivated brilliance spreading far and wide, with all things looking up together to its radiance; his penetrating wisdom circulates everywhere, and every auspicious thing attains full flourishing. No place is so secluded that it is not reached, none so distant that his influence does not arrive. Such was his radiance in the four quarters. Among the places where the royal enterprise began, none was nearer than the western lands. There we see his transforming influence, bringing order and harmony, gloriously displaying his all-encompassing benevolence; his beneficence in bringing settled security inspired praise for its intimate presence. His excellent reputation was trusted, and his brilliant light was beheld. Such, in turn, was his manifest virtue in the western lands.

Thus, of the western lands it is said that his virtue was “manifest,” and of the four quarters that it was “radiant.” This does not mean that radiance falls short of manifestation; the terms merely describe his influence in places distant and near. There was indeed reason for Heaven’s Mandate and the hearts of the people to converge upon King Wen’s virtue! Moreover, if we examine how Zhou came to possess all under Heaven, Hou Ji began the undertaking, and Gong Liu, King Tai, and King Ji continued it. This accumulation and establishment were not the work of a single morning or evening. Yet receiving Heaven’s Mandate to possess all under Heaven began with King Wen. Hence, in the three chapters of the Great Declaration (Tai shi), the words commanding the lords and exhorting the assembled host repeatedly return to King Wen’s virtue, revealing the foundation of Heaven’s aid and the people’s allegiance. The virtue and beneficence of the ancestors can thus be envisioned. The house of Zhou inaugurated a royal tenure of eight hundred years and endured longest among the Three Dynasties that possessed the Way. How true this is!

天地同運而峻烈垂焉固不必銘諸旂常九鼎
其增重矣雖曰陳行者休父也而命之以就緒
===
者則天王之光訓也是其大信與日月相昭而
洪勲集焉固不必勒諸金石九廟其嬗休矣夫
知王道之大則其內修也爲有本知王功之大
則其外攘也爲無敵又孰敢貪天功爲己力乎
嘗考宣王中興於雲漢則敬天矣於鴻鴈則勤
民矣於嵩高烝民則任相矣於采芑六月則任
將矣其所以基大命者固本於王猷而羣賢之
助亦不可誣也故曰王者得賢臣而弘功業
天命玄鳥降而生商宅殷土芒芒古帝命
punctuated:
行師，有以炳經畧之幾焉，擴懷綏之度焉，大信之懋昭，王道之蕩蕩也。蠢爾徐夷，叛兹淮土，昔嘗憑陵我華夏矣，今則孚乃神化，稽首以輸忱，不待招之自來也；昔嘗阻距我聲教矣，今則革彼奇袤，傾心以効順，不待約之自同也。是功也，非吾王之功而疇功乎？雖曰修戎者皇父也，而命之以敬戒者，則天子之丕靈也。是其至誠與天地同運，而峻烈垂焉，固不必銘諸旂常，九鼎其增重矣。雖曰陳行者休父也，而命之以就緒者，則天王之光訓也。是其大信與日月相昭，而洪勳集焉，固不必勒諸金石，九廟其媲休矣。夫知王道之大，則其內修也為有本；知王功之大，則其外攘也為無敵。又孰敢貪天功為已力乎？嘗考宣王中興，於《雲漢》則敬天矣，於《鴻鴈》則勤民矣，於《嵩高》《烝民》則任相矣，於《采芑》《六月》則任將矣。其所以基大命者，固本於王猷，而群賢之助亦不可誣也。故曰：「王者得賢臣而弘功業。」

translation_en:
…When he put his army into action, he illuminated the crucial workings of strategy and enlarged his capacity to cherish and pacify others. His great trustworthiness shone forth resplendently: how broad was the kingly Way! Those unruly Yi of Xu rebelled in the lands of the Huai. Once they had oppressed our Huaxia; now, won over by his wondrous transforming influence, they bowed their heads to the ground and offered their sincerity. Without awaiting a summons, they came of themselves. Once they had resisted our civilizing instruction; now they reformed their waywardness [?] and wholeheartedly pledged obedience. Without awaiting a compact, they joined in unity of themselves. Whose achievement could this be, if not our king’s?
Although it was Huangfu who prepared the forces, the command to act with reverence and vigilance expressed the Son of Heaven’s mighty spiritual power. His utmost sincerity moved together with Heaven and Earth, and his towering achievements were handed down. There was surely no need to inscribe them upon the banners: the Nine Tripods had already gained in weight and dignity. Although it was Xiufu who drew up the ranks, the command to bring the work to completion was the heavenly king’s illustrious instruction. His great trustworthiness shone together with the sun and moon, and vast merits accumulated. There was surely no need to engrave them on metal and stone: the nine ancestral temples shared in their glory.
Understanding the greatness of the kingly Way, we see that his cultivation of internal affairs had a firm foundation; understanding the greatness of the king’s achievements, we see that his repulsion of external enemies was invincible. Who, then, would dare appropriate Heaven’s achievement as his own strength? I have examined King Xuan’s restoration: “The Milky Way” (Yunhan) shows his reverence for Heaven; “The Wild Geese” (Hongyan), his solicitude for the people; “The Lofty Mountain” (Songgao) and “The Multitudes” (Zhengmin), his appointment of ministers; and “Gathering Millet” (Caiqi) and “The Sixth Month” (Liuyue), his appointment of generals. The means by which he established the foundation of the great Mandate were certainly rooted in royal planning, yet the assistance of the many worthy men cannot be denied. Thus it is said: “A king obtains worthy ministers and thereby enlarges his achievements.”
Heaven commanded the dark bird to descend and give birth to Shang, which dwelt in the vast lands of Yin. Of old, the Lord on High commanded…

text:
同考試官知縣劉批聖人與子尊王之義
此作詳盡且詞嚴正而意懇惻有養之士也
考試官侍讀張批謹嚴

春秋於君嗣之生也謹其名於王儲之會也嚴
其分夫禮莫大於名分此春秋於子同之生子
鄭之會而正名定分之意著矣夫子同者桓公
之嫡也凡諸侯之子必誓于王而後立同未之
誓也曷為乎書盖國有長君社稷之福此易所
===
為重長男也是故有太宰之接有卜士之負有
太史之名有士妻之食禮不為不重矣不然主
鬯承祧國誰與寄將賤得以妨貴少得以陵長啓禍
釁而滋厲階如之何其可也春秋不惟書其名
又從而目之以為同之生也國之本也顧累葉
之宗胤將微而三家之私黨益熾所以防微杜
漸絕覬覦之萌焉爾故曰謹其名者此之謂也

而後會鄭未之告也曷為乎書盖一有元良萬

translation_en:
Associate Examiner Liu, District Magistrate, comments: “This composition fully explains the sage’s principle of recognizing the son and honoring the king. Its language is grave and upright, and its sentiments earnest and compassionate. Its author is a man of cultivated character.”
Examiner Zhang, Reader-in-waiting, comments: “Careful and rigorous.”
Examiner Liao, Expositor-in-waiting of the Hanlin Academy, comments: “Based on Zhao Fang’s Collected Commentaries, it grasps the essential meaning.”
The Spring and Autumn Annals is scrupulous about the designation used when recording the birth of a ruler’s heir, and strict about distinctions of rank when recording a royal heir’s attendance at a meeting. Nothing in ritual is more important than proper designations and distinctions of rank. Thus, in its accounts of the birth of the son Tong and the meeting attended by the son Zheng, the Annals makes manifest its intention to rectify designations and establish distinctions of rank. Tong was Duke Huan’s legitimate heir. A son of a feudal lord must be formally pledged before the king before being established as heir. Tong had not yet been so pledged: why, then, was he recorded? A state’s possession of an eldest son to become its ruler is a blessing for its altars of soil and grain. This is why the Book of Changes accords such importance to the eldest son. Thus there was the Grand Steward to receive him, an officer selected by divination to carry him, the Grand Scribe to record his name, and an officer’s wife to nurse him. The ritual provisions were certainly weighty. Otherwise, to whom could the state entrust responsibility for the sacrificial spirits and the ancestral succession? Those of low status would be able to obstruct those of high status, and the younger to overbear the elder, opening the way to calamity and multiplying the causes of disaster. How could this be permissible? The Annals not only records his name but also expressly identifies him as the son, regarding Tong’s birth as fundamental to the state. Yet the lineage that had continued for successive generations was destined to weaken, while the private factions of the three houses grew ever more powerful. The purpose was therefore to guard against the slightest beginnings of disorder, arrest their growth, and extinguish the first stirrings of ambitions to usurp. This is what is meant by being scrupulous about his designation.
Zheng was King Hui’s legitimate heir. A son of the king, the Son of Heaven, must be announced to the king [?] before attending a meeting. Zheng had not yet been so announced: why, then, was he recorded? For once there is a worthy principal heir, the myriad…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
國以貞此禮所為重元子也是故有師保之詔
有疑丞之訓有左右之規有啓居之箴禮不為
不尊矣不然撫軍監國君誰與貳將上失則陵
下失則抗褻等威而瀆寵靈如之何其可也春
秋不惟殊其會又從而地之以為鄭之儲也天
下之本也顧列國之盟牲未歃而兩周之包茅
不供所以別嫌明微樹禮義之坊焉爾故曰嚴
其分者此之謂也噫以此為訓則君嗣重與子
之法明矣王儲尊匡君之義盡矣厥後莊公弗
===

他日又曰三桓之子孫微矣蓋悼魯也又曰齊

國以貞，此禮所為重元子也。是故有師保之詔，有疑丞之訓，有左右之規，有啓居之箴，禮不為不尊矣。不然，撫軍監國，君誰與貳？將上失則陵，下失則抗，褻等威而瀆寵靈，如之何其可也？《春秋》不惟殊其會，又從而地之，以為鄭之儲也，天下之本也。顧列國之盟牲未歃，而兩周之包茅不供，所以別嫌明微，樹禮義之坊焉爾。故曰嚴其分者，此之謂也。噫！以此為訓，則君嗣重，與子之法明矣；王儲尊，匡君之義盡矣。厥後莊公弗克踐申繻之言，而襄王克靖子帶之難。故孔子他日又曰：「三桓之子孫微矣。」蓋悼魯也。又曰：「齊桓正而不譎。」蓋予桓也。嗚呼！聖人謹名定分之意益章章矣。

translation_en:
…states are thereby set aright: this is why ritual places such importance on the eldest son. Thus there are admonitions from his preceptors and guardians, instructions from his advisers and assistants, remonstrances from his attendants, and injunctions concerning his rising and retiring. The ritual treatment accorded him could hardly be more exalted. Otherwise, to whom could the ruler entrust the duties of his deputy in overseeing the army and acting as regent? Failings on the part of those above would lead to encroachment, and failings on the part of those below to defiance, profaning the distinctions of rank and dishonoring august favor. How could this be acceptable? The Spring and Autumn Annals not only singles out his attendance at the meeting but also specifies its location, regarding Zheng as the royal heir and the foundation of all under Heaven. Yet before the blood of the covenant sacrifice among the states had been sipped, the bundled thatch due to the two Zhou courts was no longer being supplied. The purpose was to distinguish potentially improper relationships, clarify subtle distinctions, and establish the barriers of ritual and righteousness. This is what is meant by strictly maintaining distinctions of status.
Ah! Taking this as instruction, the ruler’s heir is accorded weight, and the rule of transmitting power to one’s son becomes clear; the royal heir is honored, and the duty of sustaining the ruler is fully discharged. Subsequently, Duke Zhuang failed to put Shen Xu’s words into practice, whereas King Xiang succeeded in quelling the rebellion of Zidai. Thus Confucius later also said, “The descendants of the three Huan lineages have declined”—surely lamenting Lu. He also said, “Duke Huan of Qi was upright and not deceitful” [?]—surely approving of Duke Huan. Alas! The sage’s intention to be scrupulous about designations and establish distinctions of status becomes ever more evident.
The duke met with the Marquis of Qi at Jiagu. The duke returned from Jiagu. Men of Qi came and returned the lands of Yun, Huan, and Guiyin. 〔All in the tenth year of Duke Ding.〕 Shusun Zhouqiu led an army to demolish the fortifications of Hou. Jisun Si and Zhongsun Heji led an army to demolish the fortifications of Bi. 〔Both in〕〔the twelfth year of Duke Ding.〕
Yang Shoulu

text:
同考試官知縣劉批是二役也孔子以禮為國
相事見諸行事之實此篇斷案明白蓋嘗究心於經
史者
考試官侍讀張批文有法度
考試官侍講學士廖批善體聖人書魯史意
春秋紀望國有化行于外而復其侵地者有化
行于內而革其僭邑者此濟西之歸三田魯邑
之墮二城而聖人以禮為國之績見矣且鄆讙
龜陰魯分地也其見侵于强齊也已久夫胡為
===
而來歸自夾谷講好兩君就壇犁彌設間萊夷
鼓譟陽飾陳牲之會陰懷伏眾之圖蓋已岌岌
乎其就危矣時則孔子以禮馭鄰辯華夏以慎
其防論神人以正其誼始則請具司馬也我為
有備而裔夷不得以肆其欺繼則力拒兵車也
彼義無詞而强國不得以開其釁於是乎景公
慙焉晏子贊之不渝盟而三田歸矣君子曰是
發也威豈在于三軍利加乎千乘特書曰來歸非
誇也紀為國之規化也孟郈費三城魯私邑

春秋紀望國，有化行于外而復其侵地者，有化行于內而革其僭邑者。此濟西之歸三田、魯邑之墮二城，而聖人以禮為國之績見矣。且鄆、讙、龜陰，魯分地也，其見侵于强齊也已久，夫胡為而來歸？自夾谷講好，兩君就壇，犁彌設間，萊夷鼓譟，陽飾陳牲之會，陰懷伏眾之圖，蓋已岌岌乎其就危矣。時則孔子以禮馭鄰，辯華夏以慎其防，論神人以正其誼。始則請具司馬也，我為有備，而裔夷不得以肆其欺；繼則力拒兵車也，彼義無詞，而强國不得以開其釁。於是乎景公慙焉，晏子贊之，不渝盟而三田歸矣。君子曰：是發也，威豈在于三軍，利加乎千乘？特書曰「來歸」，非誇也，紀為國之規化也。孟、郈、費三城，魯私邑
translation_en:
Associate Examiner Liu, Magistrate, comments: In these two undertakings, Confucius governed through ritual propriety; his assistance in affairs is manifest in actual deeds. This essay reaches clear judgments: its author has evidently devoted careful study to the Classics and histories.
Examiner Zhang, Reader-in-waiting, comments: The writing has method and measure.
Examiner Liao, Academician Expositor-in-waiting, comments: It aptly captures the sage’s intent in writing the history of Lu.
The Spring and Autumn Annals records the affairs of a preeminent state: sometimes its transforming influence spread abroad, enabling it to recover encroached-upon territory; sometimes that influence operated within, enabling it to reform towns that had usurped prerogatives. Such were the return of the three territories west of the Ji River and the demolition of the walls of two towns in Lu. In these events, the sage’s achievements in governing through ritual propriety become apparent. Yun, Huan, and Guiyin were lands allotted to Lu, and powerful Qi had long encroached upon them. Why, then, were they returned?
At Jiagu, where friendly relations were to be affirmed, the two rulers ascended the platform. Li Mi laid a trap, and the Lai tribesmen beat drums and shouted. Outwardly, the gathering was presented as a meeting with sacrificial animals arrayed; secretly, it concealed a plan to deploy hidden troops. The situation was already precariously close to disaster. At this moment Confucius used ritual propriety to manage relations with the neighboring state. He distinguished the people of the central states from outsiders to maintain the boundary carefully, and expounded the obligations owed to spirits and men to establish what was right. First, he requested that a military commander be provided: our side was thus prepared, and the outlying tribes could not give free rein to their deceit. Next, he firmly rejected the war chariots: the other side had no argument grounded in righteousness, and the powerful state could not initiate hostilities. Duke Jing was consequently ashamed, and Yanzi supported this course. The covenant was not violated, and the three territories were returned.
The gentleman says: In this exercise of power, did authority depend upon the three armies, or advantage upon bringing a thousand chariots to bear? The Annals expressly writes, “came to return.” This is no boast; it records the norms and transforming influence of governing a state. The three walled towns of Meng [?], Hou, and Fei were privately held towns within Lu …

其見據于强家也滋甚夫孰得而墮諸自陪臣
擅命三桓浸微侯犯舍甲公山揚戈私室擅維
城之固侯邦啓覆隍之虞蓋已浸浸乎其趨弱
矣時則孔子以禮定國嚴冠屨以辨其等別堂
廉以秩其分始因季孫之有問也舉法制以告
之而家不藏甲繼因仲由之爲宰也昭信義以
孚之而民可即戎於是乎季孫患焉叔孫倡之
不旋師而二城墮矣君子曰是舉也邑無百雉
之專家無百乘之僭直書曰墮非幸也紀强家
===
之見化也噫聖人俄頃之化而内外咸孚如此
非至德其孰能之語曰齊一變至於魯魯一變
至於道固也夫何齊饋女樂季孫惑焉圍成弗
克孟孫拒之蓋聖人以天自處其所能者人也
而其所不能者亦天也故曰知我者其惟春秋
乎
禮記
故人情者聖王之田也
李希賢

punctuated:
其見據于强家也滋甚，夫孰得而墮諸？自陪臣擅命，三桓浸微，侯犯舍甲，公山揚戈，私室擅維城之固，侯邦啓覆隍之虞，蓋已浸浸乎其趨弱矣。時則孔子以禮定國，嚴冠屨以辨其等，別堂廉以秩其分。始因季孫之有問也，舉法制以告之，而家不藏甲；繼因仲由之爲宰也，昭信義以孚之，而民可即戎。於是乎季孫患焉，叔孫倡之，不旋師而二城墮矣。君子曰：「是舉也，邑無百雉之專，家無百乘之僭。」直書曰「墮」，非幸也，紀强家之見化也。噫！聖人俄頃之化，而内外咸孚如此，非至德，其孰能之？語曰：「齊一變至於魯，魯一變至於道。」固也。夫何齊饋女樂，季孫惑焉；圍成弗克，孟孫拒之？蓋聖人以天自處，其所能者人也，而其所不能者亦天也。故曰：「知我者，其惟《春秋》乎！」

《禮記》
故人情者，聖王之田也。
李希賢
translation_en:
…Their occupation by powerful families had become increasingly entrenched; who could bring about their demolition? Once the retainers of those families arrogated authority to themselves, the Three Huan lineages gradually declined. Hou Fan quartered armed men [?], and Gongshan raised his weapons. Private houses monopolized the security afforded by fortified cities, exposing the lord’s state to the danger of its walls collapsing into the moat. It was already slipping steadily into weakness.

At this juncture Confucius used ritual to stabilize the state. He strictly distinguished cap from shoe to clarify rank, and differentiated the hall from its lower edges to order the respective stations of men. First, when Jisun questioned him, he explained the established laws, under which noble households were not to stockpile armor. Then, when Zhong You served as household steward, he made trustworthiness and righteousness manifest to win the people’s confidence, so that they could be called to arms. Jisun thereupon grew concerned, and Shusun took the lead: before the troops returned, two cities had been demolished.

The gentleman says: “Through this undertaking, no city could assert independence behind walls a hundred zhi in extent, and no household could usurp authority by maintaining a hundred chariots.” The unqualified entry “demolished” does not record a stroke of luck; it records the transformation of powerful families through moral influence. Ah! The sage’s transforming influence worked in so brief a time, yet those within and beyond the state alike submitted in trust. Who but someone of consummate virtue could have accomplished this? The Analects says: “With one transformation, Qi could reach the level of Lu; with one transformation, Lu could attain the Way.” Indeed so.

Why, then, when Qi presented female musicians, was Jisun beguiled by them? Why did the siege of Cheng fail, with Mengsun resisting it? The sage took Heaven as the measure of his own position: what he could accomplish belonged to the human sphere, while what he could not accomplish rested with Heaven. Thus he said: “Will it not be through the Spring and Autumn Annals that I am understood?”

Book of Rites
“Thus human feelings are the field cultivated by the sage king.”
Li Xixian

Trace the beginnings of what issues from the human heart, and make manifest the work cultivated by the sage-kings. Since the sages take human feelings as the basis of government, do they not regard people’s feelings as their own field of work? Such is the way the author of “The Conveyance of Rites” (Liyun) elaborates upon the teaching that cultivates the Way. For governing a state, nothing is better than ritual; in cultivating ritual, nothing takes precedence over rightness. Could the sages’ means of governing people lie outside these?
Thus, being still at birth is the essential condition of human nature; responding and thereby becoming engaged is the manifestation of feelings. There are joy and anger: through contact with things, beauty and ugliness become apparent in contrast. There are sorrow and delight: stirred by desires, the deviant and the correct stand opposed. The sages know that the feelings of all under Heaven are diverse in this way. They therefore personally undertake the labor, regarding others as themselves and tirelessly comforting and encouraging them. They reflect upon themselves, regarding themselves as others, and administer encouragement and correction with a fear of falling behind.
Having established safeguards, they go on to regulate and restrain these feelings, removing what is old and planning for what is new. It is as though, attending to their fields, they have already diligently opened the land for cultivation [?], yet have no respite from going to the lowlands and the field boundaries. Having expounded the teachings, they go on to bring people to find joy and repose in them, guarding against excess and moderating what is unrestrained. It is like laboring at agriculture: having already deepened the field channels and larger ditches, they must still attend to cutting grass and clearing trees.

text:
作樂也不知其懋勲崇業措民物於平康然後
樂從而作有以運合同之化焉人見其觀象於
履而制禮也不知其立綱陳紀奠邦家於熈皞
然後禮從而制有以秩品節之經焉是故以言
乎其功也彌綸參賛所過者化而所存者神斯
可以言大矣繇是比音而樂之九叙惟歌皆富
有之形容也盡善盡美而無一之或議盖大樂
與天地同和矣不其備乎以言乎其治也體統
綱維所操者約而所及者廣斯可以言辯矣繇
是比體而節之百禮既洽皆至敬之流通也有
情有文而無一之少偏盖大禮與天地同節矣
不其具乎是知禮樂之有隆殺治功之有大小
也聞樂見禮者可以考矣抑聞之五行不相沴
則王者可以制禮矣四靈以為畜則王者可以
作樂矣盖言有其位有其德有其時也乃若虞
廷之樂周官之禮燦然與天地相為昭焉而聖
德神功萬世如見豈不然哉

translation_en:
…and created music. They do not know that he first achieved magnificent accomplishments and elevated his undertakings, settling the people and all creatures in peace and well-being. Only then was music created, thereby bringing about the transforming influence of harmony and unity. People see that he contemplated the image of the hexagram Lü (Treading) and instituted ritual. They do not know that he first established guiding principles and set forth rules, securing the realm in radiant harmony. Only then was ritual instituted, thereby ordering the enduring norms of rank and measured distinction.

Thus, to speak of his accomplishments: they encompassed all things and assisted the transforming work of Heaven and Earth; wherever he passed, transformation followed, and wherever he remained, his influence was numinous. These accomplishments may indeed be called great. Accordingly, sounds were arranged to make music, and the nine fields of ordered achievement were celebrated in song: all gave expression to his abundant attainments. Perfect in goodness and beauty, with nothing open to criticism—great music indeed shares the harmony of Heaven and Earth. Is it not complete? To speak of his governance: in its coherent organization and guiding framework, what he grasped was simple, yet its reach was broad. It may indeed be called discerning. Accordingly, bodily movements were coordinated and regulated, and the hundred rites were fully harmonized: all expressed the free flow of utmost reverence. Possessing both inward feeling and outward form, with not the slightest deviation—great ritual indeed shares the measured order of Heaven and Earth. Is it not fully furnished?

From this we know that the greater or lesser elaboration of ritual and music corresponds to the greater or lesser scale of governance and accomplishment. Those who hear the music and witness the rites can examine this for themselves. Moreover, I have heard that when the Five Phases do not injure one another, the king may institute ritual; when the Four Numinous Creatures are kept as domestic animals, the king may create music. This means that he possesses the requisite position and virtue, and that the proper time has arrived. As for the music of the court of Yu and the rites of the Offices of Zhou, they shine brilliantly together with Heaven and Earth. Their sagely virtue and wondrous accomplishments remain as though visible through ten thousand generations. Is this not so?

至誠之道，天道也。天無妄，至誠亦無妄。無妄則聖矣，聖則神矣，神則不知其所以然矣。不知其所以然而然，則性性爲能存神也，物物爲能過化也。神而化之，其爲功也，至大而無外也，至廣而無際也。雖聖神，亦不自知其至此極也。故曰：至誠之道，天道也。天何爲哉？太極動而生陽，靜而生陰。其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉；其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。夫至大也，而亦至易也；至廣也，而亦至簡也。易簡之道，合一不測

The way of utmost sincerity is the Way of Heaven. Heaven is free from falsity, and utmost sincerity is likewise free from falsity. Freedom from falsity brings sageliness; sageliness brings spiritual efficacy; with spiritual efficacy, one does not know how things come to be so. When things come to be so without one knowing how, fully realizing each nature enables one to preserve spiritual efficacy, and fully realizing each thing enables one to transform wherever one passes. Spiritually efficacious and transformative, its achievement is supremely great, with nothing outside it, and supremely vast, without a boundary. Even the sage endowed with spiritual efficacy does not himself know that he has reached this ultimate point. Thus it is said: the way of utmost sincerity is the Way of Heaven. What does Heaven do? title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
也一故神兩故化也至誠無妄焉者也聖人者
法象乎天而已矣知天命於我也性也誠之源
也我之率夫性也道也誠斯立焉於是乎存養
之於未發之中太極之靜也誠以立體也省察
之於既發之和太極之動也誠以達用也誠以
立體而崇德以象易焉所以致其中者至矣誠
以達用而廣業以象簡焉所以致其和者至矣
然而體用一源也動靜一幾也易簡一理也廣

廣大而天下之功成矣繇是以中感中而大中
應焉以和召和而大和應焉以三辰則順軌矣
以五緯則協度矣以百嘉則咸鬯矣以四靈則

和位育之功至此極矣夫聖人豈自殊於人哉

…Because it is one, it is numinous; because it is two, it transforms. This is utmost sincerity, free of falsity. The sage simply takes Heaven as his model. He knows that what Heaven has ordained in him is his nature, the source of sincerity; following that nature is the Way, through which sincerity is established. Thus, preserving and nurturing the equilibrium before feelings arise corresponds to the stillness of the Supreme Ultimate: sincerity establishes the substance. Examining and scrutinizing the harmony after feelings arise corresponds to the movement of the Supreme Ultimate: sincerity brings its functioning to full expression. Through sincerity he establishes the substance and exalts virtue, modeling himself on ease; thus his bringing equilibrium to fulfillment reaches its utmost. Through sincerity he brings functioning to full expression and broadens his undertakings, modeling himself on simplicity; thus his bringing harmony to fulfillment reaches its utmost. Yet substance and functioning have one source; movement and stillness share one incipient impulse; ease and simplicity embody one principle; breadth and greatness converge upon one end; equilibrium and harmony constitute one Way. This is utmost sincerity, free of falsity.

Thus, in bringing equilibrium and harmony to fulfillment, he fathoms the numinous and understands transformation; through ease and simplicity, the principles of all under Heaven are apprehended. When equilibrium and harmony reach fulfillment, his abiding presence is numinous, and wherever he passes transformation occurs; through breadth and greatness, the work of all under Heaven is accomplished. Hence equilibrium stirs equilibrium, and supreme equilibrium responds; harmony summons harmony, and supreme harmony responds. The three celestial luminaries—the sun, moon, and stars—follow their proper courses; the five planets accord with their prescribed measures; all flourishing things thrive; and the four auspicious creatures are all nurtured together. The Supreme Ultimate is sincerity. Sincerity…

text:

不動其體則中也發而爲情動皆中節其用則
和也情不出乎喜怒哀樂之常而實原於天命
人心之正本之於不睹不聞而推至於達道達
德自達道達德而歸之於無聲無臭至易簡也
天地萬物之所以位育者以此聖人之所以爲
聖人而盡經綸參贊之責者以此夫人孰不欲

translation_en: …so flourishing that nothing can be added to it. Why speak of equilibrium and harmony? Stored within as human nature, still and unmoving, its substance is equilibrium; expressed as feelings, with every movement attaining its proper measure, its operation is harmony. These feelings do not go beyond the ordinary emotions of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure, yet they truly originate in the correctness of Heaven’s mandate and the human heart. Taking as its foundation what is neither seen nor heard, it extends to the universally followed Way and universally practiced virtues; from this Way and these virtues it returns to what has neither sound nor scent. It is supremely easy and simple. Through this, Heaven and Earth take their proper places and the myriad things are nurtured; through this, the sage becomes a sage and fulfills his responsibility to order the world and assist the transforming and nourishing work of Heaven and Earth. Who would not wish the governance of the world to match that of the sage completely, and be satisfied only then? Where it does not fully do so, this is simply because the effort to follow one’s nature has in some cases attained its utmost and in others has not. For governance of the world that proceeds from the exercise of private cleverness and unaided strength is the work of those who depart from their nature and turn their backs on the Way. Although their achievements may for a time appear evident, their governance brings only modest peace and immediate advantage; it cannot be called the highest attainment. Only when it proceeds from Heaven, follows human nature, and is cultivated through the Way can its achievements bring transformations as inexhaustible as those of Heaven and Earth. None but the sage can participate in this. The sage is one who fully realizes his nature and thereby reaches Heaven’s mandate. A single principle flows everywhere, forming an undivided whole without any gap. Its presence in me is like its presence in the myriad things; its presence in the myriad things is like its presence in Heaven and Earth. The transformations of Heaven and Earth are unfathomable, and the sage’s transforming influence is likewise unfathomable. The sage’s heart is one with Heaven. At its beginning, transformation emerges from the numinous; at its end, it enters the numinous, and the sage accompanies it throughout. When…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
乎天地旣位萬物旣育而聖人之所謂範圍而
不過曲成而不遺者亦莫得而言矣蓋嘗論之
天地設位陰陽成矣萬物散殊變化見矣聖人
成位乎其中易簡得矣是何也天道不息而運
行乖序者其變也地道有終而流峙失度者其
變也人物莫不各遂其生而或頗僻而不中疵
癘而災害者其變也聖人能以一心應之約之
於喜於怒於哀於樂而凡慶賞刑威與民憂樂
之政皆有以使之各循其性以不失其常而又
===
裁成輔相之以濟其所變則天地萬物之所不
能盡者聖人盡之矣故夫三光得其全也四時
協其序也山川鬼神亦莫不歆且宅也百姓泰
和也萬國咸寧也昆蟲草木跂行喙息萌芽孕
育莫不榮滋嘉鬯而不櫝且殈也協氣薰蒸甘
露降焉醴泉出焉器車成焉鳳皇麒麟在郊棷
焉龜龍在宮沼焉諸福之物可致之祥莫不群
趨而畢赴矣於乎聖人位育之功其神妙一至
此哉蓋能是者盡其性以同乎天地萬物而已

punctuated: 乎天地旣位，萬物旣育，而聖人之所謂範圍而不過、曲成而不遺者，亦莫得而言矣。蓋嘗論之：天地設位，陰陽成矣；萬物散殊，變化見矣；聖人成位乎其中，易簡得矣。是何也？天道不息，而運行乖序者，其變也；地道有終，而流峙失度者，其變也；人物莫不各遂其生，而或頗僻而不中、疵癘而災害者，其變也。聖人能以一心應之，約之於喜、於怒、於哀、於樂，而凡慶賞刑威、與民憂樂之政，皆有以使之各循其性，以不失其常，而又裁成輔相之，以濟其所變，則天地萬物之所不能盡者，聖人盡之矣。故夫三光得其全也，四時協其序也，山川鬼神亦莫不歆且宅也，百姓泰和也，萬國咸寧也，昆蟲草木、跂行喙息、萌芽孕育，莫不榮滋嘉鬯，而不櫝且殈也。協氣薰蒸，甘露降焉，醴泉出焉，器車成焉，鳳皇麒麟在郊棷焉，龜龍在宮沼焉，諸福之物、可致之祥，莫不群趨而畢赴矣。於乎！聖人位育之功，其神妙一至此哉！蓋能是者，盡其性以同乎天地萬物而已。
translation_en:
…when Heaven and Earth have taken their proper positions and the myriad things have been nurtured, the sage’s achievement—what is called encompassing all without exceeding due bounds, and bringing each thing to fulfillment without overlooking any—likewise lies beyond words. I have considered this: Heaven and Earth establish their positions, and yin and yang take shape; the myriad things spread out in their diversity, and transformations become manifest; the sage takes his place among them, and ease and simplicity are attained. Why is this? The Way of Heaven never ceases, yet movements that depart from their proper sequence are its aberrations. The Way of Earth brings things to completion, yet flowing waters and standing mountains that exceed their proper bounds are its aberrations. People and other beings all fulfill their lives, yet instances of perversity that miss the mean, and of disease and pestilence that bring calamity, are their aberrations. The sage can respond to these with his single mind, bringing them into order through joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure. All his measures of celebration and reward, punishment and awe, and sharing the people’s sorrows and joys enable each being to follow its nature without losing its normal course. Moreover, he regulates and assists them to remedy their aberrations. Thus, what Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things cannot fully accomplish, the sage accomplishes for them.

Accordingly, the three luminaries attain their full brilliance; the four seasons accord with their proper sequence; the spirits of mountains and rivers all delight in the offerings and rest in their abodes; the common people enjoy peace and harmony; and the myriad states are all tranquil. Insects, plants, and trees, creatures that crawl or breathe through mouths, and all that sprout, gestate, or hatch flourish abundantly and freely, without failing in birth [?] or having their eggs break before hatching. Harmonious vital energies suffuse the world; sweet dew descends; sweet springs emerge; wondrous vessels and carriages take shape [?]. Phoenixes and qilin appear in the outlying thickets, and turtles and dragons in palace ponds. All things that bring blessings and all auspicious signs that may be summoned hasten together and arrive in their entirety. Ah! Can the spiritual subtlety of the sage’s achievement in establishing proper positions and nurturing life reach such heights! Those capable of this simply fulfill their nature to become one with Heaven, Earth, and the myriad things.

punctuated:
衆人之心與聖人同也，使修之而與聖人□□，則俛仰之間、語黙嚬笑之際，豈不足以官隂陽而府萬物哉？其不能是者，私蔽之也。此其所以必有待於聖人也。周子之論順化也，其言曰：「天道行而萬物順，聖德修而萬民化。大順大化，不見其迹，莫知其然之謂神。」夫治而至於萬民化，治之極也，而必始之以聖德之修。盡天道，所以率性；盡人道，所以立教也。故曰：「化而裁之之謂變。」又曰：「天地變化，聖人效之。」其斯之謂乎？夫人言神化而足□謂聖人爲不可及者，是不達性命之原者也。豈惟不知聖人，抑亦不知天甚矣！

表

擬聖駕臨御重華殿，恭和宣宗章皇帝御製豳風圖詩，賜輔臣謝表。

楊周
translation_en:
The minds of ordinary people are the same as those of sages. If they cultivate them and become [two illegible characters] in relation to the sages [?], then, in looking down or up, speaking or remaining silent, frowning or smiling, would they not be fully capable of administering yin and yang and governing the myriad things? Their inability to do so comes from being obscured by selfishness. This is why they must depend upon the sages.

In Master Zhou’s discussion of accord and transformation, he says: “When the Way of Heaven operates, the myriad things accord with it; when sagely virtue is cultivated, the myriad people are transformed. Perfect accord and perfect transformation leave no visible traces; no one knows how they come about. This is what is called numinous.” When government reaches the point at which all the people are transformed, it has attained its utmost perfection; yet it must begin with the cultivation of sagely virtue. Fully realizing the Way of Heaven is the means of following one’s nature; fully realizing the human Way is the means of establishing instruction. Thus it is said: “Transforming and shaping things is called change.” It is also said: “Heaven and earth change and transform; the sages emulate them.” Is this not what these sayings mean? Those who speak of numinous transformation and [unclear text] regard sagehood as unattainable do not comprehend the source of human nature and destiny. Not only do they fail to understand the sages; profoundly indeed do they fail to understand Heaven!

Memorial

Draft memorial of thanks on the occasion of His Majesty’s visit to Chonghua Hall, where he respectfully composed poems matching the rhymes of Emperor Xuanzong Zhang’s imperially composed Poems on Illustrations of the Airs of Bin and bestowed them upon his grand secretaries.

By Yang Zhou.

On the twenty-seventh day of the fifth month of the thirteenth year of Jiajing, we, your servants, humbly received the favor of Our Emperor’s taking his seat in the Southern Palace, reverently composing a matching poem to Emperor Xuanzong Zhang’s ‘Poem on Viewing a Map of the Realm,’ and bestowing it upon us. punctuated:
聖人法象於天地，必稽古以考文；王者統馭乎華夷，宜宅中而圖大。粤軒轅肇分星土，肆顓頊幽贊坤靈。堯文昭煥于海隅，巍巍乎惟天爲大；舜化熙和于宇甸，鎬鎬乎如日之升。殊方範禹鼎之儀，絶域景湯圍之式。獒來西旅，陳王會以登歌；雉獻越裳，測川祇而作頌。聿觀彤管之記，堪裨丹扆之箴。
天啟皇明，上膺曆數；地連華夏，中列輿圖。振古所未聞，於今爲獨盛。恭惟宣宗章皇帝，弘紹高皇之峻烈，遹崇文考之成規。東暘谷，西流沙，悉傾心以貢篚；南丹垠，北玄漠，胥稽首以薦琛。神武懋昭，聖謨廣運，乃乘
translation_en:
…The sage takes Heaven and Earth as his models and must therefore examine antiquity to assess its cultural institutions; the sovereign governs the Chinese and the peoples beyond and should therefore dwell at the center and plan for greatness. Xuanyuan first apportioned the lands according to the stars; Zhuanxu then subtly assisted the spiritual powers of Earth. Yao’s civilizing virtue shone as far as the corners of the seas: lofty indeed, with Heaven alone matching his greatness. Shun’s transforming influence brought radiant harmony throughout the realm: bright indeed [?], like the rising sun. Distant regions supplied the forms cast upon Yu’s tripods; remote lands admired Tang’s example in opening his hunting enclosure. Mastiffs came from the western Lü: the royal assembly was recorded and celebrated in song. Pheasants were presented by Yueshang: the spirits of the rivers were fathomed [?] and hymns composed. These records of the vermilion brush may indeed supplement the admonitions addressed to the vermilion throne.
Heaven inaugurated the august Ming, which received from above the ordained succession to rule; its territory encompasses the Chinese lands, arrayed at the center of the map of the realm. Now we reverently enjoy the reign of Your Majesty the Emperor. Your Way reaches the nine heavens; your achievements rank with the Three Powers—Heaven, Earth, and humanity. You order the enduring human relationships and disseminate imperial instruction, bringing centrality and harmony to fruition; you promote rites and music to secure the imperial plan, bringing supreme concord and transformation. In accord with the seasons, you abundantly nurture life and move the world toward peace and harmony. Just as the sun first enters the Quail’s Head celestial station, we welcome the arrival of your imperial carriage. Clouds part over Yongtai; the fragrant southern breeze harmonizes with the song of relief from suffering and abundance. The sun shines upon Chonghua; the Northern Dipper ladles out the vital breath of the celestial pivot. In serving Heaven, you esteem perfect sincerity above all; in emulating your ancestors, you give precedence to pure filial devotion…

…Azure ritual cups symbolize the dark mystery [?], the vessels possessing the plain substance of earthenware and gourds; the brilliant brush displays “flying-white” calligraphy, its writing forming patterns like the Milky Way. We rejoice that all enjoy springtime under the principle that the people are one’s siblings and all things one’s companions, and that the Chinese within and the non-Chinese beyond are brought under a single rule. Your favor reaches us through gifts of fans: the tortoise presents the Plan and the horse bears the Chart. Your transforming influence spreads as you let your robes hang down in effortless rule: the dragon appears in Qian, and the tiger’s markings shine forth in Ge, the hexagrams of the Creative and Revolution.

We, your servants, present counsel at the Yellow Gate and look reverently toward your embroidered throne. We lay out maps and registers like those of Xiao He, answering above to the highest ministers; we report calamities and auspicious signs like Li Hang, attending below to the needs of the ministerial cauldron. Delighted to behold the phoenix of Shun’s court, we wish to present the Zhou court’s hymn “Wild Ducks and Gulls.”

We humbly hope that you will surpass the Five Emperors and transcend the Three Kings, unite the realm and govern its myriad beings; attain the utmost loftiness and illumination and achieve breadth and greatness; tread the path of centrality and rectitude and delight in peace and harmony. …the imperial ancestor’s plans, instructions, and glorious achievements are fully recorded in the Veritable Instructions and the Veritable Records. The learning of the sages is manifest in the classics; the government of the sages is manifest in the histories. As for what is manifest in the classics, their excellent plans and admirable instructions shine together with the sun and moon. Myriad generations follow them without daring to transgress them. The Book of Documents says: “There are established norms and rules to be handed down to descendants.” Is this not what it means? As for what is manifest in the histories, their abundant merits and lofty achievements share the greatness of Heaven and Earth. Myriad generations preserve them, and they cannot be altered. Our imperial ancestor surpassed the Three Sovereigns in the Way and exceeded the Five Emperors in achievement. The Collected Writings Composed by the Emperor investigates the cycles of the celestial bodies and the seven luminaries, tracing the origins of cosmic patterns. It inquires into the height and depth of the two powers, Heaven and Earth, elucidating the subtleties of cosmic cycles and numerical order. These teachings draw upon the Book of Changes.
The Imperial Commentary on the Great Plan begins with the five phases, the five personal affairs, the eight affairs of government, and the five regulators of time, unfolding the substance of the August Ultimate. These teachings draw upon the Book of Documents.
The Comprehensive Instructions for Aiding the World (Zishi tongxun) strictly distinguishes the ranks of ruler and minister, superior and subordinate, grounding them in the full realization of benevolence and reverence. It sets out provisions for scholars, farmers, artisans, and merchants, extending the practice of loyalty and reciprocity. These teachings draw upon the Great Learning.
The Collected Rites of the Great Ming regulates sacrifices to Heaven, Earth, and the hundred spirits, comprehending the principles of the unseen and visible realms. It arranges the forms of the five categories of rites, including auspicious and mourning rites, establishing safeguards for moral instruction. These teachings draw upon the Analects and the Mencius.
Ah! Our imperial ancestor’s words thus serve as a model for all under Heaven through the generations, and his deeds as their standard. He truly brought together the canonical teachings of the ancient emperors and kings and perfected them in their entirety. 宗廟之禮大矣！自仁率親，等而上之，至於祖；自義率祖，順而下之，至於禰。是故君子以仁處禮，則祭不疏且怠焉；以義處禮，則祭不數且煩焉。故曰：「仁人之事親也如事天，事天如事親。」然則禘也者，其仁人之盡孝乎？祫也者，其孝子之盡仁乎？禘祫兼行，其道不悖，其仁人孝子之盡義乎？
夫禘曷為者也？真德秀曰：「萬物本乎天，人本乎祖。人有此身，出於父母也；父母出於祖，祖又出於始祖，始祖又出於厥初生民得姓受氏之祖。雖年代悠遠，自根而榦，自榦而枝，其本一而已。」是故禘之為言諦也，以審諦厥先，而追禘所自出之祖也。然而有大禘焉，有時禘焉。
禮小記曰：「王者禘其祖之所自出，而以其祖配之。」蓋五年再閏，天道大備，惟天子得以行之。如虞夏商周之禘于黃帝、帝嚳，是已。夫是之謂大禘。曷謂時禘？禮燕居曰：「嘗禘之禮，所以仁昭穆也。」蓋孟
translation_en:
Great indeed are the rites of the ancestral temple! Guided by benevolence, one follows the bonds of kinship upward, rank by rank, to the ancestors; guided by righteousness, one follows the ancestral line downward in order, to the deceased father. Thus, when the gentleman conducts rites with benevolence, his sacrifices are neither infrequent nor negligent; when he conducts rites with righteousness, his sacrifices are neither excessively frequent nor burdensome. Hence it is said: “The benevolent person serves his parents as he serves Heaven, and serves Heaven as he serves his parents.” Is the di sacrifice, then, the benevolent person’s fullest expression of filial devotion? Is the xia collective ancestral sacrifice the filial son’s fullest expression of benevolence? When di and xia are both performed without conflict between their principles, is this the fullest expression of righteousness by the benevolent person and the filial son?
What, then, is the di sacrifice? Zhen Dexiu said: “All things have their origin in Heaven; human beings have their origin in their ancestors. A person’s body comes from his parents; his parents come from his ancestors; those ancestors in turn come from the founding ancestor; and the founding ancestor comes from the ancestor who, at the first beginnings of the people, acquired a surname and received a clan name. Though the ages stretch far into the past, from root to trunk and from trunk to branches, the source is one and the same.” Thus di means ‘to examine closely’: one carefully examines one’s forebears and reaches back through the di sacrifice to the ancestor from whom the founding ancestor sprang. There are, however, both the great di sacrifice and the seasonal di sacrifice.
The “Lesser Record” chapter of the Record of Rites says: “The king offers the di sacrifice to the ancestor from whom his founding ancestor sprang, and associates his founding ancestor with him in the offering.” In five years there are two intercalary months, and the cycle of Heaven reaches its full completion; only the Son of Heaven may perform this rite. The sacrifices offered by Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou to Huangdi and Diku are examples of this. This is what is called the great di sacrifice. What is meant by the seasonal di sacrifice? The “Confucius at Leisure” chapter of the Record of Rites says: “The rites of the chang and di sacrifices are the means of expressing benevolence toward the ancestors in the zhao and mu ranks.” For in the first month…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
夏而禘天道盛陽雖昭穆亦升而享焉如
閔公之禘于莊公是已夫是之謂時禘乃
若鄭玄謂禘兼郊廟劉歆又以為彌遠彌
尊張純謂禘審昭穆王肅又以為殷祭甚
大其他如高堂隆如馬融如賈逵如徐邈
如柳冕如徐道娛如孫惠蔚其為說也罔
恊而其為禮也無别折衷之者其儀禮乎
曰天子及其祖之所自出方慤别註云禘
非四時之常祭故謂之間祀以其及祖之
===
所自出故謂之追享以其比常祭為特大
故謂之大祭以其猶事生之有養故謂之
肆獻祼嗚呼茲論也其知仁人之盡孝乎
夫祫曷為者也陳祥道曰天子春礿而三
時皆祫祭之日禮交動乎上樂交應乎下
自再祼以至九獻其禮非一處自致神以
至送尸其樂非一次是故祫之為言合也
以升祔合食而各序其尊卑之位也然而
有大祫焉有時祫焉曷謂大祫禮曾子問

…in early summer the di sacrifice is performed, when yang is flourishing in the course of Heaven; even the ancestors of the zhao and mu generations are brought up to receive offerings. Such was Duke Min’s di sacrifice to Duke Zhuang. This is what is called the seasonal di sacrifice. Zheng Xuan held that di encompassed both the suburban and ancestral-temple sacrifices; Liu Xin further considered that the more distant the ancestor, the greater the reverence due. Zhang Chun held that di clarified the zhao and mu generational order, while Wang Su regarded it as an exceptionally grand, plenary sacrifice. Others, such as Gaotang Long, Ma Rong, Jia Kui, Xu Miao, Liu Mian, Xu Daoyu [?], and Sun Huiwei, offered explanations that did not agree, while failing to distinguish the rites involved. Might the Ceremonies and Rites provide an authoritative resolution? It says: “The Son of Heaven reaches back to the ancestor from whom his founding ancestor issued.” Fang Que’s separate commentary says: “The di sacrifice is not a regular sacrifice of the four seasons, and is therefore called an intervening sacrifice. Because it reaches back to the ancestor from whom the founding ancestor issued, it is called a retrospective offering. Because it is exceptionally grand compared with regular sacrifices, it is called a great sacrifice. Because it resembles providing sustenance when serving the living, it is called the presentation of offerings and libations.” Ah! Does not this explanation show an understanding of how the benevolent fulfill their filial devotion?
What, then, is the xia sacrifice? Chen Xiangdao says: “The Son of Heaven performs the yue sacrifice in spring, and in all three other seasons performs the xia sacrifice.” On the day of sacrifice, ritual actions unfold in succession above, while music responds in succession below. From the second libation through the ninth presentation of offerings, the rites are performed in more than one place; from summoning the spirits through escorting out their personator, the music has more than one sequence. Thus xia means ‘joining’: the ancestors are brought up and associated together to share the offerings, each arranged in the place appropriate to his relative rank. There is, however, both a great xia sacrifice and a seasonal xia sacrifice. What is meant by the great xia sacrifice? The ‘Questions of Zengzi’ chapter of the Record of Rites…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
曰當七廟五廟無虛主袷祭于祖祝迎四
廟之主盖三年置閏天道小備合已毀未
毀之主而饗之如商之大享于先王是已
夫是之謂大袷曷謂時袷王制曰天子犆
礿袷禘袷嘗袷烝盖三時用袷天道流行
合三昭三穆之主而饗之如周之孝享于
公先王是已夫是之謂時袷乃若張純謂
骨肉合食鄭玄又以為列尸之祀韓愈謂
祖孫尊屈史玄燦又以為服畢之祭其他
===
如顏真卿如王舉如張璪如陳京如孫抃
如元絳如張師顏其為說也罔協而其為
禮也無别折衷之者其惟春秋乎曰大有
事于太廟公羊傳云大有事者何大袷也
大袷者何合食也毀廟之主皆陳于太祖
未毀廟之主皆升合食于太祖嗚呼兹論
也其知孝子之盡仁乎愚又考之朱熹釋
禘有曰先王報本追遠之意莫深於禘非
仁孝誠敬之至不足以與此而又著為
