…says: “When the seven temples or the five temples are involved, no spirit tablet is absent. At the combined sacrifice in the ancestral temple, the Invocator welcomes the spirit tablets of the four temples.” An intercalary month is inserted every three years, marking a minor completion of Heaven’s cycle. The spirit tablets from temples already dismantled and those still standing are brought together and offered a feast, as in the Shang dynasty’s great offering to the former kings. This is what is called the great combined sacrifice (da xia). What is the seasonal combined sacrifice? “Royal Regulations” says: “The Son of Heaven performs the spring sacrifice separately, and combined sacrifices in summer, autumn, and winter.” Combined sacrifices are thus used in three seasons, following the unfolding of Heaven’s cycle. The spirit tablets of the three zhao and three mu generations are brought together and offered a feast, as in the Zhou dynasty’s filial offerings to the dukes and former kings. This is what is called the seasonal combined sacrifice.
As for Zhang Chun, he described it as blood relatives sharing a meal; Zheng Xuan regarded it as a sacrifice with an array of ancestral impersonators. Han Yu spoke of the respective honor and deference of ancestors and descendants, while Shi Xuancan regarded it as a sacrifice upon the completion of mourning. Others, such as Yan Zhenqing, Wang Ju, Zhang Zao, Chen Jing, Sun Bian, Yuan Jiang, and Zhang Shiyan, offered explanations that did not agree, while making no distinctions in their ritual prescriptions. Is it not the Spring and Autumn Annals alone that can adjudicate among them? It says: “A great sacrificial service was held at the Grand Ancestral Temple.” The Gongyang Commentary says: “What is a great sacrificial service? It is the great combined sacrifice. What is the great combined sacrifice? It is sharing a meal. The spirit tablets from dismantled temples are all set out in the temple of the founding ancestor; those from temples still standing are all brought up to share a meal in the founding ancestor’s temple.” Ah! Does not this account understand how a filial son fulfills benevolence to the utmost?

text:
考試官侍講學士廖批曆紀天辰律候地氣
惟
聖天子建中和之極天地官矣此篇究極象數亦探本之論也
天地有自然之象數惟聖人則之則其象
以治曆也所以授民時也則其數以制律
也所以宣民和也是故天地有元運焉知
元運則元象可得而求矣弗昭諸運弗測
諸象則其為術也畸而不齊天地有元聲
焉知元聲則元數可得而求矣弗協諸聲
===
弗稽諸數則其為樂也乖而不倫是故昭
運者中測象者明協聲者和稽數者神非
天下之至聖其孰能與於此夫曆冥焉而
始也軒轅氏迎日推策顓頊氏司天屬神
吾固不得而徵也惟帝堯命羲和布四時

translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Liao, Academician Expositor-in-waiting: The calendar records the celestial bodies; the pitch standards register the vital energies of the earth. Only when the sage Son of Heaven establishes the supreme standard of equilibrium and harmony do Heaven and Earth perform their offices [?]. This essay thoroughly investigates images and numbers and also seeks out their fundamental basis.

Heaven and Earth possess naturally occurring images and numbers, which only the sage takes as his models. He models himself on their images to regulate the calendar, thereby making the seasons known to the people; he models himself on their numbers to establish the pitch standards, thereby spreading harmony among the people. Thus Heaven and Earth possess primordial cycles: by understanding these cycles, one can seek out their primordial images. Unless one elucidates the cycles and measures the images, one’s methods will be partial and inconsistent. Heaven and Earth possess primordial sounds: by understanding these sounds, one can seek out their primordial numbers. Unless one harmonizes the sounds and examines the numbers, one’s music will be discordant and disordered. Thus one who elucidates the cycles attains equilibrium; one who measures the images attains clarity; one who harmonizes the sounds attains harmony; and one who examines the numbers attains spiritual insight. Who but the utmost sage under Heaven could participate in this?

The beginnings of calendrical science lie in obscurity. Xuanyuan observed the rising sun and calculated with counting rods; Zhuanxu administered celestial affairs and assigned duties to the spirits. These things I cannot substantiate. Emperor Yao, however, commanded Xi and He to lay out the four seasons. Through the Bird, Fire, Xu, and Mao constellations, they observed the course of Heaven; through sunlight, intersections, the moon’s final darkness, and the new moon [?], they examined what was fitting for the earth. Their directions for beginning work, making adjustments, bringing tasks to completion, and putting things in order all served simply to make the seasons known to the people. Had they not grasped the primordial cycles of Heaven and Earth? Thus the Seven Regulators were brought into alignment, and the five celestial bodies moved in succession. The Xia calendrical reckoning was duly ordered, and the Yin calendar was renewed [?]. The people of Zhou took these as their models, and thereupon …

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
是乎有馮相以叙天位有保章以掌天星
治曆亦爲詳矣乃若漢曆則鄧平之三統
也編訢之四分也劉洪之乾象也唐曆則
傅仁均之戊寅也李淳風之麟德也徐承
嗣之貞元也徐昂之宣明也宋曆則吳昭
素衛朴之乾元奉元也吳處訥周琮之應
天明天也史序宋行古之儀天崇天也皇
居卿姚舜輔之觀天占天也其爲術也畸
而不齊會而通之者其惟一行乎其論推
===
步氣朔也凡七曰中朔也發斂也日躔也
月離也軌漏也交會也五星躔度也其議
曆數也十有二曰曆本也中氣也合朔也
滅沒也卦候也卦氣也日度也日躔也九
道也晷漏中星也日蝕也五星也蓋一行
以大衍爲主合二始以位剛柔合二中以
通律曆合二終以紀閏餘以合朔定日月
之會以日度正周天之數以中星正二十
四氣以卦氣定七十二候郭守敬獨宗其

…thus there were Astrologers (Fengxiang) to order the celestial positions and Astronomers (Baozhang) to oversee the stars; the regulation of the calendar had also become elaborate. As for the Han calendars, there were Deng Ping’s Three Systems (Santong) calendar [?], Bian Xin’s Quarter-Remainder (Sifen) calendar, and Liu Hong’s Celestial Images (Qianxiang) calendar. Among the Tang calendars were Fu Renjun’s Wuyin calendar, Li Chunfeng’s Linde calendar, Xu Chengsi’s Zhenyuan calendar, and Xu Ang’s Xuanming calendar. Among the Song calendars were the Qianyuan and Fengyuan calendars of Wu Zhaosu and Wei Pu; the Yingtian and Mingtian calendars of Wu Chune and Zhou Cong; the Yitian and Chongtian calendars of Shi Xu and Song Xinggu; and the Guantian and Zhantian calendars of Huang Juqing [?] and Yao Shunfu. Their methods were disparate and inconsistent. Was it not Yixing alone who brought them together into a coherent whole?

His treatment of calculating the seasonal qi and new moons comprised seven sections: mean solar terms and new moons; the unfolding and gathering of seasonal qi; the sun’s course; the moon’s motion; orbital tracks and water-clock measurements; conjunctions; and the degrees traversed by the five planets. His discussion of calendrical computation comprised twelve sections: the foundations of the calendar; the principal solar terms; conjunctions at the new moon; the obliteration and disappearance of fractional remainders; hexagrams and seasonal periods; hexagrams and seasonal qi; solar degrees; the sun’s course; the nine paths; sundial and water-clock measurements and culminating stars; solar eclipses; and the five planets.

Yixing took the Great Expansion (Dayan) as his basis. He combined the two beginnings to assign positions to the hard and the soft; combined the two middles to connect the pitch standards with the calendar; and combined the two endings to record the remainders requiring intercalation. He used new-moon conjunctions to determine the meetings of sun and moon, solar degrees to establish the correct numerical measure of the celestial circuit, culminating stars to correct the twenty-four solar terms, and the correspondence of hexagrams with seasonal qi to determine the seventy-two seasonal periods. □□三者凡七則自冬至以至日行創法
□□七則自日行以距白道其亦知元運
與元象爾矣乎夫律奚爲而始也伊耆氏
之土鼓葦籥軒轅氏之截管制律吾亦不
得而徵也惟帝舜命后夔審六律直溫剛
簡本天性也詩歌聲律協人情也而夫以
擊以拊以詠以閒凡以宣民和而已其得
天地之元聲乎是故五聲旣正八音克諧
大夏由忠大濩從質周人監之於是乎有
===
樂德樂語樂舞以敎國子有六律六同六
德以命太師制律亦已精矣乃若漢樂則
夏侯寬之十七章也李延年之十九章也
京房之六十律也唐樂則祖孝孫之十二
和也李紓之九章也顏師古之九舞也徐

之于慶曆也胡瑗王洙之于皇祐劉几楊
傑之于元豐也其爲樂也乖而不倫□□

punctuated: □□三者，凡七則，自冬至以至日行；創法□□七則，自日行以距白道。其亦知元運與元象爾矣乎？夫律奚爲而始也？伊耆氏之土鼓葦籥，軒轅氏之截管制律，吾亦不得而徵也。惟帝舜命后夔，審六律，直溫剛簡，本天性也；詩歌聲律，協人情也。而夫以擊以拊，以詠以閒，凡以宣民和而已，其得天地之元聲乎？是故五聲旣正，八音克諧。大夏由忠，大濩從質，周人監之。於是乎有樂德、樂語、樂舞以敎國子，有六律、六同、六德以命太師，制律亦已精矣。乃若漢樂，則夏侯寬之十七章也，李延年之十九章也，京房之六十律也；唐樂，則祖孝孫之十二和也，李紓之九章也，顏師古之九舞也，徐彥伯之十二曲也；宋樂，則竇儼、宋白之于建隆也，阮逸、李照之于景祐也，范鎭、房庶之于慶曆也，胡瑗、王洙之于皇祐，劉几、楊傑之于元豐也。其爲樂也，乖而不倫□□

…[two illegible characters] the three [?], comprising seven rules, from the winter solstice through the sun’s motion; the newly devised methods [two illegible characters] comprise seven rules, from the sun’s motion to its distance from the moon’s path [?]. Did he, too, know only the primordial cycles and celestial configurations? How, then, did the pitch standards originate? As for Yiqi’s earthen drums and reed pipes, and Xuanyuan’s cutting pipes to establish pitch standards, I can find no evidence to verify them. Emperor Shun, however, commanded Hou Kui to examine the six pitch standards. Uprightness, warmth, firmness, and simplicity were rooted in innate nature; poetry, song, tones, and pitch standards accorded with human feelings. Striking and tapping, singing and alternating instrumental passages—all served simply to give expression to harmony among the people. Did this capture the primordial sound of Heaven and Earth? Thus, once the five tones were correctly established, the eight classes of musical instruments could sound in harmony. The Great Xia music proceeded from wholehearted devotion, and the Great Huo music followed unadorned substance; the people of Zhou took these as their models. Accordingly, they used musical virtues, musical language, and musical dances to instruct the sons of the state’s elite, and charged the Music Master with the six yang pitch standards, the six yin pitch standards, and the six virtues. The establishment of pitch standards had already attained great refinement.

As for Han music, there were Xiahou Kuan’s seventeen compositions, Li Yannian’s nineteen compositions, and Jing Fang’s sixty pitch standards. For Tang music, there were Zu Xiaosun’s Twelve Harmonies, Li Shu’s nine compositions, Yan Shigu’s nine dances, and Xu Yanbo’s twelve pieces. For Song music, there were the efforts of Dou Yan and Song Bai during the Jianlong era; Ruan Yi and Li Zhao during the Jingyou era; Fan Zhen and Fang Shu during the Qingli era; Hu Yuan and Wang Zhu during the Huangyou era; and Liu Ji and Yang Jie during the Yuanfeng era. Their music was discordant and lacked proper order [two illegible characters]…

text:
通之者其惟元定乎其論律吕本原也十
有三曰黃鍾體數也黃鍾用數也黃鍾生
十一律也十二律之實也變律也律生五
聲也變聲也八十四聲也六十調也候氣
也審度也嘉量也謹權衡也其述證辨也
凡十曰造律也律圍徑也黃鍾之實也損
益相生也和聲也五聲小大之次也變宫
變徵也六十調也候氣也度量權衡也蓋
元定以黃鍾爲元在聲爲中聲在氣爲中
===
氣在人爲中和其宫聲圍徑則取諸漢斛
之積分宫徵變調則取諸禮䟽之緒論積
寸積分則取諸遷固之成書變聲半聲則

旋宫下篇則自聲律名義以至法數其亦
知元聲與元數爾矣乎愚嘗觀諸易矣易
革之象曰澤中有火革君子以治曆明時
夫水性潤下火性炎上氣相息則天地革

通之者，其惟元定乎？其論律吕本原也，十有三：曰黃鍾體數也，黃鍾用數也，黃鍾生十一律也，十二律之實也，變律也，律生五聲也，變聲也，八十四聲也，六十調也，候氣也，審度也，嘉量也，謹權衡也。其述證辨也，凡十：曰造律也，律圍徑也，黃鍾之實也，損益相生也，和聲也，五聲小大之次也，變宫變徵也，六十調也，候氣也，度量權衡也。蓋元定以黃鍾爲元，在聲爲中聲，在氣爲中氣，在人爲中和。其宫聲圍徑，則取諸漢斛之積分；宫徵變調，則取諸禮䟽之緒論；積寸積分，則取諸遷固之成書；變聲半聲，則取諸杜佑之通典。朱子獨稱其闡究精微，又與門人訂正，上篇則自陰陽辰位以至旋宫，下篇則自聲律名義以至法數。其亦知元聲與元數爾矣乎？

translation_en:
…was it perhaps Yuanding alone who comprehended them? His discussion of the origins of the pitch standards has thirteen sections: the fundamental number of Huangzhong, the Yellow Bell pitch; its operative number; its generation of the other eleven pitch standards; the capacities of the twelve pitch pipes; altered pitch standards; the generation of the five notes from the pitch standards; altered notes; the eighty-four notes; the sixty modes; observing qi; examining measures of length; standardizing measures of capacity; and carefully regulating weights and balances. His exposition of evidence and distinctions has ten sections: constructing pitch pipes; their circumferences and diameters; the capacity of the Huangzhong pipe; mutual generation through diminution and augmentation; harmonizing notes; the ordering of the five notes by magnitude; the altered gong and altered zhi notes; the sixty modes; observing qi; and measures of length, capacity, and weight.
Yuanding took Huangzhong as the origin: in sound it is the central tone, in qi it is the central qi, and in human beings it is equilibrium and harmony. For the circumference and diameter associated with the gong note, he drew upon the calculated volume of the Han hu measure; for modal changes involving gong and zhi, upon the discussions in the subcommentaries on the ritual classics; for volumes calculated in cun and fen, upon the completed histories of Sima Qian and Ban Gu; and for altered notes and half-length pitches, upon Du You’s Comprehensive Institutions (Tongdian). Master Zhu singled him out for praise for investigating and elucidating the finest subtleties, and also worked with his disciples on corrections. The upper part extends from yin and yang and the positions of the twelve chronograms to the rotation of tonal centers; the lower part, from the names and meanings of notes and pitch standards to methods and numbers. Did he, too, understand the primordial sound and primordial number, and no more?
I have examined this in the Book of Changes. The Image commentary on its hexagram Ge, “Change,” says: “Within the lake there is fire: Change. The noble man accordingly regulates the calendar and clarifies the seasons.” Now water by nature moistens and descends, while fire by nature blazes and rises. When their qi displace one another, Heaven and Earth undergo change …

之次也牛宿艮位也星紀之次也日月交
會于此合璧曜靈是天地之元運也而亦
元象之所斡旋也是故聖人觀其象而曆
作焉然而欲測象以昭運其說有三一曰
觀五星以測三垣二曰觀三垣以測二十

…and the four seasons are brought to completion. Commentators hold that the lunar lodge Xu occupies the position of the trigram Kan and belongs to the celestial station Xuanxiao; the lunar lodge Niu occupies the position of the trigram Gen and belongs to the celestial station Xingji. Here the sun and moon meet in conjunction, joined like paired jade discs and shining with radiance. This is the primordial cycle of Heaven and Earth, and it is also what the primordial celestial configurations turn and regulate. Thus the sages observed these configurations and devised the calendar. To measure the configurations and thereby elucidate the cycle, however, there are three methods: first, observe the five planets to measure the Three Enclosures; second, observe the Three Enclosures to measure the twenty-eight lunar lodges; third, observe the twenty-eight lunar lodges to determine the central solar terms. These, too, are things that those seeking to understand the primordial cycle ought to know.

Once thunder stirs, Heaven and Earth move in accord, and the four seasons do not go astray. Commentators hold that when thunder and rain arise, this constitutes the hexagram Jie, Release, and all things burst their seed coats; when thunder and lightning arrive, this constitutes the hexagram Feng, Abundance, and the five vital energies all flow freely. text:
測也而斡旋元氣以昭元運非聖人莫之
能也其惟堯之欽若爾矣乎夫元數可求
也而統會元數以協元聲非聖人莫之能
也其惟舜之克諧爾矣乎恭惟我
皇上紹
堯廣運邁
舜重華
純心建中和之極
峻德兼制作之全是宜曆正于上而五星聚室
===
天不愛其道矣樂作于下而萬靈咸格人
不愛其情矣易曰天垂象聖人則之禮曰
聖人作樂以應天愚也端有望于
今日
第四問
李希賢
同考試官教諭楊批真西山以四事論名臣事
業經生類能言之此篇有取於武侯宣公而歸本於其
學術可以占所養矣

業經生類能言之此篇有取於武候宣公而歸本於其

同考試官教諭楊　李希賢
punctuated:
測也，而斡旋元氣以昭元運，非聖人莫之能也，其惟堯之欽若爾矣乎！夫元數可求也，而統會元數以協元聲，非聖人莫之能也，其惟舜之克諧爾矣乎！恭惟我皇上紹堯廣運，邁舜重華，純心建中和之極，峻德兼制作之全。是宜曆正于上，而五星聚室，天不愛其道矣；樂作于下，而萬靈咸格，人不愛其情矣。《易》曰：「天垂象，聖人則之。」《禮》曰：「聖人作樂以應天。」愚也端有望于今日。
第四問
李希賢
同考試官教諭楊批：真西山以四事論名臣事業，經生類能言之。此篇有取於武侯、宣公，而歸本於其學術，可以占所養矣。
translation_en:
…can be measured; yet none but a sage can direct the primordial vital force and thereby make manifest the primordial cycles. Was this not precisely Yao’s reverent conformity to Heaven? Primordial numbers can be ascertained; yet none but a sage can bring them into a unified whole and thereby harmonize the primordial sounds. Was this not precisely Shun’s achievement of harmony?
We reverently consider how Our Emperor carries forward Yao’s far-reaching sway and surpasses Shun’s successive splendor. With a pure heart, he establishes the supreme standard of centrality and harmony; with lofty virtue, he possesses the full capacity to institute rites and music. It is fitting, then, that the calendar is set right above and the five planets gather in the lunar lodge Shi: Heaven withholds nothing of its Way. Music arises below and the myriad spirits all arrive: people withhold nothing of their feelings. The Book of Changes says, “Heaven displays its images, and the sage takes them as his model.” The Book of Rites says, “The sage creates music to respond to Heaven.” In my ignorance, I assuredly place my hopes in the present day.
Fourth Question
Li Xixian
Comment by Associate Examiner Yang, Instructor: Zhen Xishan discussed the achievements of eminent ministers under four headings, and students of the classics can generally expound these. This essay draws upon Marquis Wu and Duke Xuan, tracing their achievements back to their learning. From it one can judge what the author has cultivated within himself.

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
考試官侍讀張批尚論古人能得真識
遺意錄之不獨以其文也
考試官侍講學士廖批真景元學術甚正通
達治體此子於終篇歸重大學衍義亦足以仰見
聖學采納之一端矣
濟天下者事功也所以濟事功者學術也
學術之係於人大矣道明而後身可誠也
身誠而後君可効也凡代天工者皆然而
况身任天下之責者乎故必有端本澄源
===
之學而後有正君定國之功否則出之無
本謀之匪臧而不足以語大人格君之業
矣此古之善輔天下者必始於正己也執
事發策以古名臣為問愚竊伏草萊國門
之外豈敢以謀
廟廊乎雖然嘗聞西山真文公矣文公以高
明純粹之學接濂洛關閩之傳生逢宋季
不究柄用故其經世之志謀國之才格君
之學見於讀書記中有不能自已者如此

事發策以古名臣爲問愚竊伏草萊囪門
之外豈敢以謀
廟廊乎雖然嘗聞西山真文公矣文公以高

不究柄用故其經世之志謀國之才格君
之學見於讀書記中有不能自已者如此
punctuated:
考試官侍讀張批：尚論古人，能得真識遺意，錄之不獨以其文也。
考試官侍講學士廖批：真景元學術甚正，通達治體。此子於終篇歸重《大學衍義》，亦足以仰見聖學采納之一端矣。
濟天下者，事功也；所以濟事功者，學術也。學術之係於人大矣！道明而後身可誠也，身誠而後君可効也。凡代天工者皆然，而况身任天下之責者乎？故必有端本澄源之學，而後有正君定國之功。否則出之無本，謀之匪臧，而不足以語大人格君之業矣。此古之善輔天下者必始於正己也。執事發策，以古名臣為問。愚竊伏草萊、國門之外，豈敢以謀廟廊乎？雖然，嘗聞西山真文公矣。文公以高明純粹之學，接濂洛關閩之傳，生逢宋季，不究柄用，故其經世之志、謀國之才、格君之學，見於《讀書記》中，有不能自已者如此。
translation_en:
Comment by Examiner Zhang, Reader: In appraising men of antiquity, he achieves genuine insight into their surviving intentions [?]. This answer is included for more than its literary merits.

Comment by Examiner Liao, Expositor-in-waiting: Zhen Jingyuan’s learning was thoroughly orthodox, and he understood the essential principles of government. This candidate, in concluding his essay, places particular weight on the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning (Daxue yanyi). This also enables us reverently to perceive one aspect of what His Majesty has drawn upon in his sagely learning.

What brings aid to the world is practical achievement; what makes practical achievement possible is learning. Great indeed is the importance of learning to a person! Only after the Way is understood can one make oneself sincere; only after making oneself sincere can one render service to the ruler. This holds for all who perform Heaven’s work on its behalf. How much more must it hold for those who personally bear responsibility for the world? Thus, learning that rectifies the root and clarifies the source must precede achievements that rectify the ruler and bring stability to the state. Otherwise, one’s actions lack a foundation and one’s plans are unsound: they fall short of what may be called the great man’s work of correcting the ruler. This is why those of antiquity who ably assisted in governing the world invariably began by rectifying themselves.

You, honored examiners, have posed a policy question concerning eminent ministers of antiquity. I, in my ignorance, dwell obscurely among the weeds beyond the capital’s gates. How could I presume to offer counsel on affairs of the imperial court? Nevertheless, I have heard of Master Zhen of Xishan, posthumously titled Wengong. Through his lofty, luminous, and pure learning, he carried forward the traditions of Lian, Luo, Guan, and Min. Born in the closing era of the Song, he was never given full scope to exercise governing authority. Thus his resolve to order the world, his ability to devise plans for the state, and his learning directed toward correcting the ruler appear in his Record of Reading (Dushu ji), expressing an impulse he could not restrain.

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
其論名臣事業也乙集所載其目有四曰
正己也曰格君也曰謀國也曰用人也先
之端本以澄其源次之達用以昭其化體
用一原内外無間大學之道其在是矣求
之於古惟皐夔稷契伊傅周召爲能盡之
春秋以還雖號爲名卿賢大夫往往知求
治而不知格心知弼違而不知養德其既
也汲汲於事功之末而謂治忽不本於人
主之身雖救過亦所不暇矣於乎大學不
===
明之弊一至是哉當漢之盛時則有若蕭
何議法畫一曹參清淨無爲丙吉深厚不
伐魏相嚴正自持不可不謂之賢也故史
稱之曰高祖開基蕭曹爲冠孝宣中興丙
魏有聲嗣是而名世者若匡衡之經術韋
玄成之文章雖云當世少雙亦一節焉已
爾以四事考之求其克盡而無歉者惟諸
葛武侯焉當其遵晦布衣高卧長嘯中心
澹泊不求聞達其正己可知隆中數語進

translation_en:
…As for its discussion of the achievements of eminent ministers, those recorded in Collection B fall under four headings: rectifying oneself, rectifying the ruler, planning for the state, and employing worthy men. First comes setting the root right to clarify the source; next comes putting this into practice to manifest its transforming influence. Substance and function share a single source, with no separation between inner and outer: herein lies the Way of the Great Learning. Among the ancients, only Gao Yao, Kui, Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao could fully realize it. From the Spring and Autumn period onward, even those acclaimed as eminent ministers and worthy grandees often knew how to seek good government but not how to rectify the ruler’s heart, how to correct his errors but not how to nurture his virtue. In the end, they busied themselves with the peripheral matters of practical achievement, supposing that order and disorder were not rooted in the ruler’s own person. They could scarcely even keep up with remedying his faults. Alas! Could the harm caused by failing to understand the Great Learning reach such a point!

At the height of the Han, there were men such as Xiao He, who deliberated on laws and established uniform standards; Cao Can, who maintained tranquility and governed through nonaction; Bing Ji, who was profound and generous without boasting; and Wei Xiang, who conducted himself with stern uprightness. They must certainly be called worthy. Thus the history praises them: “When Gaozu laid the foundations, Xiao and Cao stood foremost; in Xiaoxuan’s restoration, Bing and Wei won renown.” Those who subsequently became renowned in their age, such as Kuang Heng for his learning in the Classics and Wei Xuancheng for his literary accomplishments, may have had few equals in their day, yet theirs was merely excellence in a single respect. Judged by these four undertakings, the only one who could fulfill them all without deficiency was Zhuge Liang, Marquis Wu. When he lived in obscurity as a commoner [?], reclining at ease and giving long, resonant whistles, inwardly tranquil and free of ambition, seeking neither fame nor advancement, his rectification of himself was evident. With a few words at Longzhong, he advanced…

延咨諏尊昭烈為帝胄之英斥吳魏為僭

正君又可知矣國歩艱難英雄睥睨提數
州之卒抗萬全之師卒能剖鼎一足屹立

之傑然者乎原侯之所以至是者學爲之
本也觀其言曰寧靜以致遠治世以大德
可見矣先儒謂其才本王佐可興禮樂覘
古伊呂寔伯仲之豈不信哉在唐之盛時
則有若房玄齡隨事效謀杜如晦臨機輒
斷姚崇應變不窮宋璟耿介有節不可不
謂之賢也故史稱之曰貞觀之治房杜有
功開元之盛姚宋繼跡嗣是而名世者若
punctuated:
延咨諏，尊昭烈為帝胄之英，斥吳魏為僭寇之國，凛然以明大義、復中原為己責，其正君又可知矣。國歩艱難，英雄睥睨，提數州之卒，抗萬全之師，卒能剖鼎一足，屹立西陲，使曹氏父子睢盱駭愕，而救敗不暇。神機竒畧，應變百出，内以修明政教，外以戢和人民，勞之而不怨，殺之而不憤焉。其風動群材，奔走知勇，不惟受任者樂為之用，雖以流徙放逐之徒，亦皆捐軀效命而弗辭，其瀘夷之約束可想見也。豈非漢臣之傑然者乎？原侯之所以至是者，學為之本也。觀其言曰：「寧靜以致遠，治世以大德。」可見矣。先儒謂其才本王佐，可興禮樂，視古伊呂，寔伯仲之，豈不信哉？
在唐之盛時，則有若房玄齡隨事效謀，杜如晦臨機輒斷，姚崇應變不窮，宋璟耿介有節，不可不謂之賢也。故史稱之曰：「貞觀之治，房杜有功；開元之盛，姚宋繼跡。」嗣是而名世者若
translation_en:
…invited to offer counsel, he honored Zhaolie as an outstanding scion of the imperial house and denounced Wu and Wei as states of usurpers and rebels. With stern resolve, he took clarifying the great principles of righteousness and recovering the Central Plain as his own responsibility. His ability to set his ruler aright is thus also evident. The state’s fortunes were troubled, and powerful rivals eyed it disdainfully. Leading the troops of a few provinces against a fully prepared army, he ultimately secured one leg of the tripartite realm and stood firm on the western frontier, leaving Cao Cao and his son staring in alarm and scarcely able to avert defeat. His inspired calculations and extraordinary strategies produced countless responses to changing circumstances. Within, he put government and moral instruction in good order; without, he brought the people under peaceful discipline. When he put them to labor, they did not resent it; when he put them to death, they felt no indignation. His influence stirred men of talent and drew the wise and brave into his service. Not only did those entrusted with office gladly serve him, but even displaced people and exiles offered their lives in loyal service without demur. From this one can imagine his discipline of the non-Han peoples of the Lu region. Was he not an outstanding minister of the Han?
If we trace how the Marquis achieved this, learning was its foundation. This is evident in his words: “Through tranquility, attain far-reaching ends; through great virtue, govern the world.” Earlier Confucian scholars said that his talents were fundamentally those of an assistant to a true king, capable of bringing rites and music to flourish, and that he ranked alongside Yi Yin and Lü Shang of antiquity. Is this not indeed true?
In the flourishing days of the Tang, there were men such as Fang Xuanling, who supplied plans suited to each affair; Du Ruhui, who made decisions whenever the moment demanded; Yao Chong, whose responses to changing circumstances were inexhaustible; and Song Jing, who was upright and steadfast in principle. They must surely be called worthy. Thus the histories praised them, saying: “For the good government of the Zhenguan era, Fang and Du deserve credit; in the prosperity of the Kaiyuan era, Yao and Song followed in their footsteps.” Those who subsequently won renown in their age included…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
裴度之勳德李德裕之才望雖云當時莫
及亦一體焉已爾以四事考之求其克全
而無愧者惟陸宣公焉方其身處禁林小
心精潔方鎮寵賂雖微必卻其正己可知
朝廷獻納動中機宜尊仁義爲治平之粱
肉黜功利爲害身之膏肓慨然以格非心
引當道爲己任其格君又可知矣平時計
畫成敗較然初問兩河淮西事宜即陳招
携悔禍至計勸上蓄威昭德居重馭輕惜
===
德宗不聽以至倉皇失措而涇原卒變及
狩奉天卒賴其謀外以感將士之泣內以
衛乘輿之安言之而輒效計之而允孚矣
其建請臺省長官各舉其屬不惟體統之
甚正雖綱目亦秩然而不煩端可垂紳委
弁而自治其名實之敷陳可考見也豈非
唐臣之傑然者乎原公之所以至是者學
爲之本也觀其言曰上不負天子下不負
所學可見矣先儒謂其學本帝師才通經

…Pei Du’s achievements and virtue, and Li Deyu’s ability and reputation, though said to have been unequaled in their time, each amounted to excellence in only one aspect. Judged by the four criteria, only Lord Lu Xuan (Lu Zhi) could fully satisfy them without cause for shame. While serving in the Hanlin Academy, he was scrupulous and pure in conduct. He invariably rejected gifts intended to curry favor from regional military governors, however small. His rectitude in his own conduct is thus evident. His advice at court invariably suited the circumstances. He esteemed benevolence and righteousness as the fine grain and meat that nourished orderly peace, and rejected the pursuit of achievement and profit as a disease lodged deep within the body. He resolutely took it upon himself to correct the ruler’s errant intentions and guide him onto the proper Way. His ability to rectify his ruler is likewise evident.

In his planning, the consequences leading to success or failure were always clear. When first consulted about affairs in Lianghe and Huaixi, he immediately presented the best plans for winning back the estranged and averting calamity. He urged the emperor to build up his authority and manifest his virtue, holding firm at the center to control the lesser powers. Regrettably, Dezong did not listen, and matters descended into panic and confusion when the Jingyuan troops mutinied. When the emperor fled to Fengtian, he ultimately relied on Lu’s counsel: outwardly, it moved officers and soldiers to tears; inwardly, it secured the emperor’s safety. Whatever Lu proposed proved effective, and whatever he planned proved dependable.

He proposed that the heads of the Censorate and the central government departments each recommend their own subordinates. This not only made the hierarchy of authority thoroughly correct; it also rendered both its general framework and its details orderly and uncomplicated. The ruler could simply sit in his ceremonial sash and cap, and affairs would be ordered of themselves. Lu’s exposition of the relationship between titles and actual responsibilities can thus be examined and understood. Was he not an outstanding minister of the Tang?

If we trace how Lord Lu attained this stature, learning was its foundation. title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
濟視漢賈誼寔度越之豈不信哉於乎二
公惟其所學者正故其事業亦正然其所
謂學者豈有他哉達聖賢帝王之道明格
致誠正之理精求其意而體之於身以之
行己則順而祥以之事君則公而溥終其
身而不變動乎物而不違古之所謂學者
亦若是焉而已或曰武侯之學足以撥亂
而不能挽炎運之微宣公之學足以正君
而不能回德宗之聽事功成就顧出蕭曹
===
諸君下焉何也曰學在己用不用時也功
在己其成其敗天也天之所命豈人所能
為哉蕭曹諸君不賢於二公而所值者豁
達大度好賢勵精之主故其同心輔政寬
嚴之相濟謀斷之相資猶足以弼漢業而
興唐祚況進而主臣俱賢者哉故上有堯
舜禹湯文武之君必有皐夔稷契伊傅周
召之臣有皐夔稷契伊傅周召之臣必有
時雍風動永綏迓衡之治元首股肱相須

而不能挽炎運之微宣公之學足以正君
而不能回德宗之聽事功成就願出蕭曹
===

在已其成其敗天也天之所命豈人所能
爲哉蕭曹諸君不賢於二公而所值者豁

興唐祚况進而主臣俱賢者哉故上有堯
舜禹湯文武之君必有皐夔稷契伊傅周
召之臣有皐夔稷契伊傅周召之臣必有
時雍風動永綏迓衡之治元首股肱相須
punctuated:
濟，視漢賈誼，寔度越之，豈不信哉？於乎！二公惟其所學者正，故其事業亦正。然其所謂學者，豈有他哉？達聖賢帝王之道，明格致誠正之理，精求其意而體之於身，以之行己則順而祥，以之事君則公而溥，終其身而不變，動乎物而不違。古之所謂學者，亦若是焉而已。
或曰：「武侯之學足以撥亂，而不能挽炎運之微；宣公之學足以正君，而不能回德宗之聽。事功成就，顧出蕭曹諸君下焉，何也？」曰：「學在己，用不用，時也；功在己，其成其敗，天也。天之所命，豈人所能為哉？蕭曹諸君不賢於二公，而所值者豁達大度、好賢勵精之主，故其同心輔政，寬嚴之相濟，謀斷之相資，猶足以弼漢業而興唐祚，況進而主臣俱賢者哉？故上有堯舜禹湯文武之君，必有皐夔稷契伊傅周召之臣；有皐夔稷契伊傅周召之臣，必有時雍風動、永綏迓衡之治。元首股肱相須
translation_en:
…statecraft; compared with Jia Yi of the Han, he truly surpassed him. Is this not credible? Ah! It was precisely because these two gentlemen’s learning was correct that their undertakings were also correct. Yet was there anything else to what they called learning? They comprehended the Way of the sages, worthies, and sovereigns, and understood the principles of investigating things, extending knowledge, making intentions sincere, and rectifying the mind. They sought the meaning of these principles with precision and embodied them in their own persons. Applying them to their conduct, they acted harmoniously and auspiciously; applying them to serving their sovereigns, they acted impartially and generously. Throughout their lives they remained unchanged; when moved by external things, they did not depart from these principles. What the ancients called learning was simply this.
Someone asks: “The learning of the Marquis of Wu [Zhuge Liang] was sufficient to quell disorder, yet he could not reverse the decline of the Han’s fiery dynastic destiny. The learning of Duke Xuan [Lu Zhi] was sufficient to rectify his sovereign, yet he could not turn Dezong’s ear toward his counsel. In their achievements, however, they fell below such men as Xiao He and Cao Shen. Why?”
The reply is: “Learning rests with oneself; whether one is employed depends on the times. Effort rests with oneself; its success or failure depends on Heaven. How could human beings determine what Heaven ordains? Such men as Xiao He and Cao Shen were no worthier than these two gentlemen, but the rulers they encountered were open-minded and magnanimous, cherished worthy men, and applied themselves energetically to government. Thus, by assisting government with a common purpose, balancing leniency with severity, and making planning and decision reinforce one another, they were still able to sustain the Han enterprise and bring prosperity to the Tang throne. How much more could be achieved when sovereign and ministers were both worthy! Thus, when there are rulers above like Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, there must be ministers like Gao Yao, Kui, Ji, Xie, Yi Yin, Fu Yue, the Duke of Zhou, and the Duke of Shao. With ministers such as these, there must be government that brings universal concord, transforms the people as wind moves them, secures enduring tranquillity, and ushers in peace. The head and the limbs—the sovereign and his ministers—depend upon one another…”

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
而成亶其然矣方今
聖天子日御
經帷進講大學衍義而輔弼之臣法從之僚
相與賛襄獻納以共成正大光明之業真
氏之學雖未少試于當時而實大行于
今日誠
宗社無疆之慶也愚也何幸身親見之
第五問
陳啓亨
===
同考試官教諭陳批吏治有關於國家
大矣此篇援漢唐馭吏之法而獨酌以變通之方必
有識之士也
同考試官教授唐批援古論今之治言有根
據法知變通他日效用明達國體非子也耶主司拭
目以俟
考試官侍讀張批人知久任爲治安良法
但情與勢格多未能行觀子之策其善濟變者乎
考試官侍講學士廖批知人安民古人定論知

translation_en:
…and thus achieve their purpose: indeed, this is so! Today our sagely Son of Heaven daily attends the imperial lectures, where the Extended Meaning of the Great Learning is expounded. His assisting ministers and attendant officials together offer support and counsel, jointly bringing to fruition an upright and enlightened undertaking. Although Master Zhen’s learning was never put even briefly into practice in his own time, it is now being implemented widely. This is truly a boundless blessing for the dynasty and the altars of state. How fortunate I, in my ignorance, am to witness it in person!

Chen Qiheng

Comment by Associate Examiner Chen, Instructor: The administration of officials is of immense consequence to the state! This essay draws upon Han and Tang methods of managing officials, yet independently weighs how those methods should be adapted to changing circumstances. Its author must be a man of discernment.

Comment by Associate Examiner Tang, Professor: You invoke antiquity to discuss governance today. Your statements are well grounded, and you understand how to adapt administrative methods. When you enter service in the future, will you not be one who thoroughly understands the principles of governing the state? The examiners eagerly await that day.

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
人在於慎銓選嚴考課安民在於選循良責久任子言
及之必識治體者
蓋聞治有機也時有宜也通其變化可裁
也宜其時然後能成功也執事發策慨然
思古循良之化而憂馭吏之難其知要哉
今天下猶一身也內而
邦畿腹心也外而郡縣四肢也民元氣也四
肢之不治而欲元氣流行於一身以保其
腹心之無虞不可得已治天下之勢何以
異此是故郡縣者政教之首也天下者郡
縣之積也治不明於郡縣其何以成天下
之治乎虞廷咨牧命辭勅治可謂厚矣必
繼之以黜陟之典周官計吏詔王受會可
謂詳矣必重之以廢置之文鼓舞人材變
通吏治自前代則已然矣故在堯舜時曰
九德咸事也百工惟時也在周文武時曰
棫樸能官人也南山有臺樂得賢也夫以
唐虞三代之盛不能去是而治何獨至於

…knowing men rests on care in selecting officials and rigor in evaluating their performance; bringing peace to the people rests on choosing conscientious, benevolent officials and requiring them to serve long tenures. You have addressed these matters and must therefore understand the essentials of government.
I have heard that government has its critical opportunities, and each age its appropriate measures. By comprehending changing circumstances, one can determine what to do; only by fitting one's actions to the times can one achieve success. You, honored examiners, have posed this policy question, earnestly recalling the transforming influence of the conscientious, benevolent officials of antiquity and expressing concern over the difficulty of managing officials. How well you understand what is essential!
Now, all under Heaven resembles a single body. Within, the capital region is its heart and abdomen; beyond, the prefectures and counties are its four limbs; the people are its vital energy. If the four limbs are out of order, one cannot expect vital energy to circulate throughout the body and keep its heart and abdomen free from danger. How does the situation in governing all under Heaven differ from this? Thus prefectures and counties are where government and moral instruction begin, and all under Heaven is the aggregate of prefectures and counties. If good government is not manifest in the prefectures and counties, how can orderly rule throughout the realm be achieved?
The court of Shun consulted the regional governors and charged them, in its commands, to govern diligently. Its solicitude could indeed be called profound, yet it necessarily followed this with procedures for demotion and promotion. Under the Zhou offices, officials' accounts were assessed and the king was advised to receive their annual reports. These arrangements could indeed be called detailed, yet they necessarily reinforced them with provisions for dismissal and appointment. Encouraging talented men and adapting the administration of officials to changing circumstances were already established practices in earlier ages.

後世而凝之漢宣帝勵精之主也躬親庶
政日以聽決為事丞相已下並加裁覈及
拜刺史守相皆親見問每臨朝歎曰庶民
所以安其田里而無歎息愁恨者政平訟
理也與我共此者其惟良二千石乎憂民
之心其切如此故杜延年名卿也出為邊
郡治效不進詰責加焉有治理效輒以璽
書勞勉增秩賜金公卿闕則選所表以用
之故在當時尹翁歸為扶風以捕盜為三
===

信臣輩皆以治行高第入為少府為大司
農若是其盛而其最先褒異荐登相侯之
貴則黃霸其人焉史稱漢宣之治優於孝
文神爵五鳳之間吏稱民安不其然乎唐
太宗願治之君也屈己親賢日以愛人為
務議郎已上引對便殿及拜都督刺史臨
軒授之嘗對侍臣曰朕思天下事丙夜不
安枕永惟治人之本莫重刺史故錄姓名

…why, then, should later ages hold it fixed and unchanging [?]? Emperor Xuan of Han was a ruler who exerted himself in government. He personally attended to the many affairs of state, making the hearing and deciding of matters his daily business, and scrutinized officials from the Counselor-in-Chief downward. When appointing Regional Inspectors, Commandery Governors, and kingdom Chancellors, he personally received and questioned them all. Whenever he held court, he would sigh and say: “What enables the common people to live peacefully on their land and in their villages, without sighs, sorrow, or resentment, is equitable government and the proper settlement of lawsuits. Who shares this task with me, if not good officials of the two-thousand-bushel rank?” Such was the depth of his concern for the people. Thus even Du Yannian, a distinguished minister, was questioned and reprimanded when, after being sent out to govern a frontier commandery, his administrative results failed to improve. Whenever officials achieved effective government, the emperor rewarded and encouraged them with letters bearing the imperial seal, increased their salary ranks, and bestowed gold. When vacancies arose among the highest ministers, he selected appointees from those whose merit had been commended. Thus, in his time, Yin Wenggui, serving as Governor of Youfufeng, ranked first among the Three Metropolitan Areas for apprehending bandits; Han Yanshou, governing Dong Commandery, ranked first in the empire for deciding judicial cases; and Shao Xinchen and others, having received the highest assessments for their administration, entered the central government as Chamberlain for the Palace Revenues or Chamberlain for the National Treasury. Such was the flourishing state of affairs. Yet the man who was first singled out for praise and distinction and repeatedly advanced to the honors of Counselor-in-Chief and marquis was Huang Ba. The histories declare that Emperor Xuan’s government surpassed that of Emperor Xiaowen, and that during the Shenjue and Wufeng reign periods officials fulfilled their duties and the people lived in peace. Was this not indeed so?

Emperor Taizong of Tang was a ruler who aspired to good government. He humbled himself and drew worthy men close, making care for the people his daily concern. He summoned officials of the rank of Court Gentleman for Consultation and above to audiences in a side hall; when appointing Area Commanders-in-Chief and Regional Inspectors, he personally presided over their investiture. He once told his attendant ministers: “Thinking about the affairs of the empire, I cannot rest easy on my pillow even in the third watch of the night. I ponder continually the foundations of governing the people: no office is more important than that of Regional Inspector.” He therefore recorded their names…

Whenever reports were submitted, the emperor sorted them by the officials’ names, assessing and recording their good and bad conduct. Whenever an appointment was to be terminated or filled, he consulted these records to determine whom to advance or remove. Thus, at that time, Li Tongke, as prefect of Bazhou, was renowned for integrity and fairness; Zhang Yunji, as magistrate of Wuyang, was renowned for benevolence and care; and Jia Dunshi and others were all summoned on account of their exceptional administrative achievements to serve as Vice Supervisors of the Heir Apparent’s Household or Grand Area Commanders. 謂世固有廉者矣未必能明廉且明矣未
必能仁或其心雖仁而短於剸裁或其才
雖贍而偏於意向兼是五者之善難爲人
才之難豈非一時傷俗之論乎仰惟我

陟之典化行俗美百六十年于兹人材輩

…with his pure virtue and distinguished reputation, came forth to serve and bring comfort to the people. He once proposed establishing eight criteria for regulating official administration: benevolence, discernment, impartiality, and integrity would distinguish the capable; harshness, cunning, greed, and cowardice would identify the bad. Surely he had perceived this problem. Master Wu of Linchuan also said: “There are certainly men of integrity in the world, but they are not necessarily discerning. Even those both upright and discerning are not necessarily benevolent. Some, though benevolent at heart, lack decisiveness; others, though abundantly talented, are biased in their inclinations. To combine the merits of these five qualities is among the greatest difficulties in finding men of talent [?].” Was this not a judgment lamenting the prevailing mores of his time?
I humbly reflect that our dynasty, in employing men, gives foremost importance to those who shepherd the people. Drawing upon the institutions of Yu and Zhou, it has clearly established rules for dismissal and promotion. Its transforming influence has spread and customs have flourished for these one hundred and sixty years. Talented men have emerged in succession; its excellent laws and benevolent intentions could not be surpassed. Recently, however, officials have gradually grown lax, and the people are weary. Though the court is diligent in exhortation and admonition, few respond with tangible achievements to the sagely sovereign’s benevolent intentions. Why is this? In my humble view, selection and appointment today lack care, and transfers and promotions occur too rapidly. Both are defects in the employment of men, but excessive speed is especially harmful. Why? If a man serving the age is devoted to the people and wishes to pursue plans for their lasting welfare, the results cannot be measured overnight. title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄
text:
議黜之矣其赫然見騰于薦牘者銓曹又
以為有功而亟擢然則是為長吏者能與
不能俱不得久也夫以民之望於吏者不
勝其厚而吏之去乎民者若是其輕彼此
相視如客主勢然此治之所以不克也漢
唐用人之法欲其久安于位既有賜予以
勞之於始又懸爵祿以持之於終不聞其
驟遷以奪其成效啓其速化以幸乎曲通
今縱未能一槩久而不遷至如居官長子
===
孫之法獨不可少推其意而調停之使稍
久於其位乎吏知其久居而不去也又有
厚望以養其志顯罰以懾其心而無復他
岐之可惑則天下之吏雖其或非盡賢皆
將黽勉赴會而求成功故為治不勞而得
循良之臣此馭吏之法也通變宜民莫踰
是矣不識執事以為然否

將黽勉赴會而求成功故爲治不勞而得
循良之臣此馭吏之法也通變宜民莫踰
是矣不識執事以爲然否
punctuated: 議黜之矣。其赫然見騰于薦牘者，銓曹又以為有功而亟擢。然則是為長吏者，能與不能俱不得久也。夫以民之望於吏者不勝其厚，而吏之去乎民者若是其輕，彼此相視如客主，勢然。此治之所以不克也。漢唐用人之法，欲其久安于位，既有賜予以勞之於始，又懸爵祿以持之於終，不聞其驟遷以奪其成效，啓其速化以幸乎曲通。今縱未能一槩久而不遷，至如居官長子孫之法，獨不可少推其意而調停之，使稍久於其位乎？吏知其久居而不去也，又有厚望以養其志，顯罰以懾其心，而無復他岐之可惑，則天下之吏，雖其或非盡賢，皆將黽勉赴會而求成功。故為治不勞而得循良之臣，此馭吏之法也。通變宜民，莫踰是矣。不識執事以為然否？
translation_en:
…they propose dismissing him. Those whose names appear prominently in recommendations, meanwhile, are judged meritorious by the Ministry of Personnel and promptly promoted. Thus those serving as local administrative heads, whether capable or incapable, are alike unable to remain long in office. The people’s expectations of their officials are exceedingly great, yet officials leave the people with such unconcern. Under these circumstances, each regards the other as guest and host. This is why effective government cannot be achieved.

The Han and Tang method of employing officials sought to keep them securely in their posts for a long time. Rewards were granted at the outset to recognize their efforts, while the prospect of rank and emoluments sustained them through to the end. We do not hear of sudden transfers depriving them of the fruits of their work, or encouraging rapid advancement through the hope of gaining access by crooked means [?]. Even if it is now impossible to make all officials remain long without transfer, could we not draw somewhat upon the intent of the practice whereby officials remained in office long enough to rear children and grandchildren, and adjust arrangements so that they stay a little longer in their posts?

If officials know that they will remain long in office rather than depart, and if generous prospects sustain their aspirations while clearly enforced punishments strike fear into their hearts, with no other paths left to tempt them, then the officials throughout the realm, though perhaps not all worthy, will strive diligently to meet the requirements and achieve results. Thus, without laborious efforts at governing, one obtains conscientious and upright officials. This is the way to manage officials. For adapting institutions to benefit the people, nothing surpasses it. I do not know whether you, honored sir, consider this correct.

嘉靖甲午秋八月，京府臣僚奏當大比畿內士，上命臣道南、臣袞特輟史事，往主校焉。錄成，臣袞當敘諸末簡，乃拜手稽首，作而颺言曰：「懿哉！我皇上作人之功，神妙一至此哉！先是，四方風俗，藝文太盛，經生學子過為眩騖之辭，驚愚詭俗，私相慕效，爾雅渾噩之風寖少衰矣。我皇上申詔禮官勸學，議令凡程式試士所取之文，必明白正大，有裨治理，
translation_en:
Postface to the Record of the Shuntian Prefecture Provincial Examination

In the eighth month of autumn in the jiawu year of Jiajing [1534], the officials of the capital prefecture memorialized that it was time to hold the triennial examination for scholars within the metropolitan region. His Majesty specially ordered your servants Daonan and Gun to suspend their historiographical duties and go to preside over the examination. When the record was completed, it fell to your servant Gun to write a postface on its final leaves. Bowing with hands raised and knocking my head to the ground, I rose and proclaimed:

“How splendid! The wondrous efficacy of our August Sovereign’s work in nurturing talent has reached such heights! Previously, throughout the realm, literary composition had flourished to excess. Students of the Classics and other scholars went too far in producing dazzling, extravagant language, startling the ignorant and astonishing the common people. Privately admiring and imitating one another, they gradually allowed the refined and unaffected literary manner to decline somewhat. Our August Sovereign again commanded the officials of the Ministry of Rites to encourage learning and deliberate upon regulations requiring that all compositions selected when examining scholars under the prescribed forms must be clear, upright, and of benefit to good government …

畢具士學爲文期以適用則古
之所謂德行道藝之教誠不出
此謂士止於文固不可而謂文
蓋不足以得士抑惑矣〔臣〕於是

或謂科目取士，藝焉已爾。臣愚以為不然。孔門四科，文學並列。詩書所載，辭命之作，雅頌之篇，彝章典則，吏方將畧，先王致治之跡，靡不燦然畢具。士學為文，期以適用，則古之所謂德行道藝之教，誠不出此。謂士止於文，固不可；而謂文盡不足以得士，抑惑矣。
臣於是竊有懼焉。宋儒蘇軾曰：「科塲之文，風俗所繫。其見錄者，間以為
translation_en:
…Florid and unfounded expressions were excluded and no longer accepted. Consequently, throughout the realm and beyond, as far as the seas, all embraced the same ethos. Within the schools, everyone came to honor classical learning and refine their understanding of the way of government; their writing steadily recovered its classical elegance.
Some say that selecting men through the examinations tests literary skill alone. Your foolish servant believes otherwise. Literary learning ranked alongside the other disciplines among the four branches of instruction in Confucius’s school. The Book of Odes and the Book of Documents contain diplomatic pronouncements, the Greater and Lesser Odes and the Hymns, enduring statutes and authoritative rules, methods of civil administration and military strategy: the traces of how the former kings achieved good government are all brilliantly displayed therein. If scholars learn to write with practical application as their aim, then what the ancients called instruction in virtuous conduct, the Way, and the arts truly falls within this scope. To say that a scholar’s accomplishments end with writing is certainly unacceptable; yet to say that writing is wholly inadequate as a means of finding worthy men is likewise mistaken.
At this, your servant privately feels apprehensive. The Song scholar Su Shi said: “Writing in the examination halls bears upon customs and manners. Those whose writings are selected, hearing of it [?], take it as …

translation_en:
…encouragement; those whom they pass over and do not select hear of it and take warning. Through a single day's decisions to reject or accept, and judgments of the relative merits of scores or hundreds of men, encouragement and admonition spread throughout the realm. The goodness or badness of scholars' habits depends upon this; the flourishing or decline of government and moral transformation depends upon it. Can one fail to exercise care? Your foolish servant lacks precision in discernment and deeply fears failing to fulfill Your Majesty's purpose in entrusting him with this duty today. Yet what I dare not withhold is my wholehearted effort; what I cannot force beyond its limits is my understanding. Even if I exert myself wholeheartedly, should men of talent nevertheless be overlooked, it would be difficult to escape blame.
Yet the responsibility of the scholars is perhaps greater still. While they are commoners dwelling in humble thatched homes, they speak grandly and advance lofty arguments, constantly aspiring to match the outstanding men of antiquity. Once their names are entered on the rolls of officeholders, scarcely one in ten can put these words into practice. Those who cast them aside like a discarded cap or childhood locks hardly need discussing. If this is so, people will seize upon their words and criticize them, saying that literary scholars are thus unsuited to practical service, and will soon…

title: 嘉靖十三年順天府鄉試錄

厚亦奚以士為而故詳延慎選

不負所學增光選舉茂翊

punctuated: 且議絀之矣。則士之自責，不有甚於主司之責士以言乎？我國家養士於學，建師崇餼，其澤甚厚。亦奚以士為，而故詳延慎選之，若是其勤且至哉？教化之行也，建首善，自京師始。士生畿輔之郡，親被聖天子之化，左右趨之，淪浹膚髓，將不有偉特瑰異之材，傑然而出，不負所學，增光選舉，茂翊昌運，以先四方者乎？《詩》有之：「思皇多士，生此王國。王國克生，維周之楨。」褒然□□□今日之畿士也。爾畿士，其益懋之，毋徒以文
translation_en:
…and will moreover propose rejecting them. Should not scholars therefore demand more of themselves than the presiding examiners demand of them through their written words? Our dynasty nurtures scholars in its schools, appointing teachers and providing generous stipends; its beneficence is very great. For what purpose does it seek scholars, that it takes such pains to invite them with care and select them cautiously, with such diligence and thoroughness? In spreading moral instruction, the establishment of the foremost model of goodness begins with the capital. Scholars born in the prefectures of the capital region personally receive the transforming influence of the sagely Son of Heaven. Turning toward it on every side, they are steeped in it to their very marrow. Will there not emerge outstanding men of magnificent and extraordinary talent, who live up to their learning, bring distinction to the selection of officials, splendidly assist this flourishing age, and lead the four quarters?
The Book of Odes says: “How splendid are the many worthy men, born in this royal realm! The royal realm can indeed produce them: they are the pillars of Zhou.” Such praise … [three illegible characters; sense uncertain] the scholars of today’s capital region [?]. You scholars of the capital region, exert yourselves still further; do not merely rely on literary composition …
